title: A Small State Machine for Reliable Email Automation
summary:
Email-driven workflows often look simple in a diagram: create a user, send a message, click a link, and mark the test as passed.

In a real CI run, the email can arrive late, a worker can retry, or a previous test can still own the inbox. The result is a flaky test with a vague error like “verification email not found.” A small state machine gives the workflow a memory and makes these failures much easier to reason about.

Why email automation needs explicit states

An email test is not only waiting for a message. It is coordinating an application, a mail delivery path, a test runner, and cleanup. Each part can move at a different speed.

Without explicit states, the test usually has a pile of booleans and sleeps:

created = true
sleep(5)
if message_exists():
    click_link()

This can pass locally and fail under CI load. It also make retries difficult because the runner does not know whether it should wait, search, or release the mailbox.

The five-state model

For many staging and end-to-end tests, five states are enough:

  1. Reserved — the run has an isolated mailbox or mailbox lease.
  2. Triggered — the application accepted the action that should send an email.
  3. Observed — the expected message was found and matched to this run.
  4. Consumed — the test used the link, token, or code successfully.
  5. Released — the mailbox and related test data can be cleaned up.

Every transition should have an event ID, a timestamp, and a run ID. The logs is much more useful when it can answer “which run owns this message?” instead of only showing that a message arrived.

The Observed state is especially important. Finding any email with the right subject is not enough. Match a correlation value in the recipient, message header, link, or body. Otherwise, an earlier retry may be mistaken for the current test.

A small implementation contract

The contract can be represented by a record that is stored next to the test run:

{
  "run_id": "checkout-1842",
  "mailbox": "qa-1842@example.test",
  "state": "triggered",
  "expected_event": "verify-account",
  "attempt": 1,
  "expires_at": "2026-10-26T06:00:00Z"
}

The worker should accept the same run_id more than once. If a retry sees Observed, it should return the existing observation instead of creating another mailbox. This is the same mental model behind idempotent email verification APIs: repeat the request, but do not repeat the side effect.

Use bounded polling instead of one long sleep. For example, check after 1, 2, 4, and 8 seconds, then record a timeout with the last known state. The exact numbers depend on the environment, but the important bit is that each wait is visible in the run log.

Retries, ownership, and cleanup

Retries should be safe at every boundary. A delivery worker may send twice, and a test runner may ask twice. Store a message or event identifier when possible, and reject a result that belongs to another run.

For password reset and login flows, versioned reset tokens in PostgreSQL show a useful related pattern: make the valid version explicit, then invalidate older values. Email tests can apply the same idea to links and codes.

For a short-lived staging check, a throwaway email generator can provide a separate inbox boundary. Keep that inbox out of production data, give it an expiration time, and never treat it as a durable user identity.

Some failure reports contain phrases such as “temp gamil com” or “tempail mail” because a tester searched with a typo. Those phrases can be useful in support notes, but they should not become an identity key or a test assertion.

Cleanup should be a state transition, not an afterthought. If the test fails after Triggered, a finalizer can still release the mailbox. If the run is already expired, the cleanup job can remove it without trying to consume a message. This is less clever, but more easier to operate.

Practical checklist

  • Give every email test a unique run ID.
  • Store an explicit state instead of relying on sleep calls.
  • Match messages to the current run, not only to a subject line.
  • Make retries return existing observations where possible.
  • Add expiration to mailbox leases, tokens, and test records.
  • Log the transition that failed and the last observed state.
  • Release test mailboxes even when the assertion fails.

The goal is not to build a large workflow engine. A small state machine is enough to turn email automation from a timing guess into a traceable developer tool. Once the states are visible, flaky tests become ordinary state transitions to inspect, retry, and improve.

title: Let's Encrypt Goes to 64-Day Certificates in February. Grep Your Server for 60, 80 and 83 First.
summary:
Let's Encrypt posted a short note on October 7 that most small SaaS founders will scroll past. Starting February 10, 2027, every certificate it issues or renews will be valid for 64 days by default, not 90. Then on February 16, 2028, it drops again to 45 days.

The post also has one line I'd tape to the monitor:

Grep for common hardcoded numbers like 83, 80 or 60 in cron jobs, wrapper scripts and runbooks if you're not sure.

That's the whole risk in one sentence. If your HTTPS renewal was set up two years ago by "past you" and has worked silently since, there's a decent chance a 60 is hiding somewhere in it. On 90-day certs that 60 left you 30 days of slack. On 64-day certs it leaves 4. On 45-day certs it renews two weeks after the cert already died.

This post is the boring checklist I'd run on a tiny SaaS before February. Most of it takes an hour.

The dates, in one place

There are two separate things changing and people mix them up.

The industry rule. The CA/Browser Forum (the group whose rules every public CA follows) passed ballot SC-081 in 2025. Max certificate lifetime for certs issued:

  • from March 15, 2026: 200 days (it was 398)
  • from March 15, 2027: 100 days
  • from March 15, 2029: 47 days

Let's Encrypt's own schedule, which runs ahead of that:

  • now: 90 days by default
  • opt-in already: the shortlived profile issues ~6-day certs, and since May 13, 2026 the tlsserver profile issues 45-day ones
  • since October 14, 2026: the staging environment already issues 64-day certs, for testing
  • February 10, 2027: default goes to 64 days
  • around May 11, 2027: the last 90-day Let's Encrypt cert expires
  • February 16, 2028: default goes to 45 days

Nothing gets revoked. You just get the shorter cert at your next renewal after each date.

If you buy certs instead (from your registrar, or a "1 year SSL" upsell), you're already on the 200-day rule. A public example: as of late October 2026, dev.to itself serves a certificate issued in November 2025 that runs until December 12, 2026. That's 397 days, issued before the cutoff. Its replacement can't be longer than 200 days, and the one after March 2027 can't be longer than 100. If someone on your team installs a bought cert by hand once a year, that turns into at least twice a year now, about four times a year from 2027, and eight or more a year from 2029. Manual stops being a plan.

Why a tiny SaaS should care more than a big one

Big companies have a platform team and a cert inventory. At 30 customers, the cert inventory is "whatever certbot did in 2024."

Two things make it worse now:

  1. Nobody emails you anymore. Let's Encrypt stopped sending expiry reminder emails on June 4, 2025. If you set things up when those emails existed, your safety net was quietly removed. Certbot's own docs still have a line saying the CA will email you, which doesn't help.
  2. Webhooks fail before customers notice. Stripe needs a valid certificate on your webhook endpoint in live mode. If the cert expires, deliveries show a TLS error and Stripe retries for up to three days. After that you're replaying events by hand, and in the meantime renewals, cancellations and failed payments aren't reaching your app. Your marketing site might be on a host that handles certs for you while api.yourapp.com sits on a VPS that doesn't.

Step 1: find out what actually renews your certs

Before grepping anything, figure out which tool is in charge. On a typical small setup it's one of these:

  • A managed host or proxy (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare, Render, Fly, a managed load balancer). They issue and renew for you. Mostly not your problem, but check any custom domains you added by hand.
  • Caddy. It handles renewal itself and has supported ACME Renewal Information (ARI) since 2.8, so it asks Let's Encrypt when to renew.
  • Certbot. Usually a systemd timer or a cron entry someone added.
  • acme.sh. A cron entry under your user.
  • Something homemade. A script, a Docker container that runs certbot once, a GitHub Action. These are the ones that bite.

On a Linux box, this finds most of them:

systemctl list-timers --all | grep -i -E 'certbot|acme'
sudo grep -rn -i -E 'certbot|acme|renew' /etc/crontab /etc/cron.d /var/spool/cron 2>/dev/null
crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -i -E 'certbot|acme|renew'
certbot --version 2>/dev/null
~/.acme.sh/acme.sh --version 2>/dev/null

Write down what you find. Seriously, one line in a notes file: "api box, certbot 2.x, systemd timer, nginx reload hook: no". You'll need it in step 3.

Step 2: grep for the hardcoded numbers

Here's what common renewal rules do on each lifetime. "Slack" is how many days are left on the old cert when renewal first tries.

Renewal rule 90-day cert 64-day cert 45-day cert
Ask the CA via ARI (about 2/3 of lifetime) ~day 60, ~30 left ~day 43, ~21 left ~day 30, ~15 left
Certbot 4.0+ default (1/3 lifetime left) day 60, 30 left ~day 43, ~21 left day 30, 15 left
Old certbot default (30 days left) day 60, 30 left day 34, 30 left day 15, 30 left
acme.sh 3.1.2 and older default (59 days after issue) 31 left 5 left expired 14 days earlier
Hand cron, --force-renewal every 60 days 30 left 4 left expired 15 days earlier
Runbook "renew at 80 / 83 days" 10 / 7 left expired expired

The "days left" rules are fine. The "days since issue" rules are the ones that break. That's what Let's Encrypt means by grepping for 60, 80 and 83.

Where to look:

# certbot: per-cert overrides (no output is good)
sudo grep -rn renew_before_expiry /etc/letsencrypt/renewal/

# acme.sh: older versions wrote Le_RenewalDays='60' into every cert's conf
grep -rn Le_RenewalDays ~/.acme.sh/
# (if you never passed --days, a 60 here is just the old default)

# anything homemade that forces renewal on a fixed schedule
sudo grep -rn -E 'force-renew|--days|renew.*(60|80|83)' /etc/cron* /var/spool/cron /etc/systemd/system ~/bin ~/scripts 2>/dev/null

A few things from the changelogs worth knowing:

  • Certbot 4.0.0 switched its default from a fixed 30 days to "renew when less than 1/3 of the lifetime is left". Certbot 4.1.0 added ARI support, and an early ARI answer wins over a later renew_before_expiry. So a recent certbot with the stock timer is basically fine. An old certbot pinned by your distro is the thing to check.
  • acme.sh changed its default from 60 days to 30 days and added ARI in 3.1.3 (April 2026). Before that, the default renewal was 60 days after issue, minus a day. If you installed it a while ago and turned off auto-upgrade, acme.sh --upgrade is step one. Then run acme.sh --info -d yourdomain.com and look at Le_NextRenewTimeStr to see when it actually plans to renew, instead of trusting what you remember.
  • If your "automation" is a cron line with --force-renewal on a fixed calendar, replace it with the plain certbot renew running twice a day. Certbot's docs recommend exactly that and say it's safe to run as often as you like, since it does nothing until a cert is due.

Step 3: renewal isn't deployment

This one gets people even with perfect timing. Certbot renews the file on disk. Nginx keeps serving the old cert from memory until it reloads. If nothing reloads it, the new cert sits there unused and the old one expires right on schedule.

With certbot, add a deploy hook. It only runs after a successful renewal:

sudo tee /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/reload-nginx.sh > /dev/null <<'HOOK'
#!/bin/sh
nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx
HOOK
sudo chmod +x /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/reload-nginx.sh

With acme.sh it's the --reloadcmd you pass when installing the cert. Their README flags it as IMPORTANT, and they're right.

Other places the new cert never reaches: a Docker image that copied the cert in at build time, a load balancer or CDN where you uploaded a cert by hand, a second server that gets the cert by rsync from the first one. On 90-day certs you might've caught that by accident. On 64-day certs, you get fewer accidents.

To test the renew-plus-hook path without touching real certs:

sudo certbot renew --dry-run --run-deploy-hooks

--dry-run talks to the staging server and doesn't save anything. Deploy hooks don't run during a dry run unless you add --run-deploy-hooks.

Step 4: check the certificate people actually get, from outside

Checking the file on disk tells you what certbot did. It doesn't tell you what browsers and Stripe see. I'd run something like this from a machine that isn't the server, once a day:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# check-certs.sh: fail if any cert you actually serve expires within DAYS days
DAYS=14
HOSTS="example.com www.example.com api.example.com status.example.com"

fail=0
for h in $HOSTS; do
  cert=$(echo | timeout 10 openssl s_client -connect "$h:443" -servername "$h" 2>/dev/null)
  end=$(echo "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -enddate 2>/dev/null | cut -d= -f2)
  if [ -z "$end" ]; then
    echo "FAIL $h: couldn't get a certificate"
    fail=1
  elif ! echo "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -checkend $((DAYS * 86400)) >/dev/null; then
    echo "FAIL $h: expires $end"
    fail=1
  else
    echo "ok   $h: expires $end"
  fi
done
exit $fail

-checkend takes seconds and exits 1 if the cert expires inside that window. -servername matters if more than one site lives on the same IP, otherwise you might be checking the wrong cert.

Pick the alert threshold for the new lifetimes. A lot of us have a "warn at 30 days left" rule from the 90-day era. On a 64-day cert renewed at about 2/3, a healthy cert hits 30 days left around day 34, roughly 9 days before renewal even tries. So the alert fires on every healthy cert, you mute it, and then it can't help you when it matters. I'd use 14 days for 64-day certs and something like 7 to 10 once you're on 45-day ones.

Where the alert goes matters as much as the check. The SideHunt guide on monitoring a side project when you can't watch it all day splits alerts into "interrupt me now" and "tonight is fine". A cert with 14 days left is a tonight one. A cert with 2 days left, or a FAIL on the webhook host, is a now one.

And the check script is itself a cron job that can die quietly. If it stops running, "no alerts" looks exactly like "everything's fine". I wrote about heartbeat checks for the jobs a tiny SaaS runs. Same idea here: ping on success so you hear about it when the check itself stops.

Step 5: find the certs you forgot about

The hostnames list in that script is only as good as your memory. Certificate Transparency logs remember better. Every public cert gets logged, so you can see every name anyone got a cert for on your domain:

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=example.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u

crt.sh is free and kind of slow, and sometimes it just returns a 502. Retry in a minute. What usually turns up: an old staging. subdomain still pointing at a box, status. on some service you set up once, a mail. cert on the mail server, a customer's custom domain. Anything still live goes into HOSTS. Anything dead, delete the DNS record so it stops being a thing.

While you're thinking about expiry dates, the domain itself expires too, and a cert check won't catch that one. The IndieHunt guide on protecting a small SaaS from account lockouts covers registrar lock, auto-renew and the "renewal emails go to the domain that expired" trap.

Step 6: if anything still renews by hand, fix that now

Two cases I'd look for:

Manual DNS challenges. If you ran certbot certonly --manual with DNS and paste a TXT record each time, certbot's docs are clear that those certs won't renew automatically unless you add auth hook scripts. Today Let's Encrypt reuses a successful validation for 30 days. From February 2027 that's 10 days, and on the 45-day schedule in 2028 it's 7 hours. So basically every renewal will need a fresh challenge. Move to a DNS plugin for your DNS provider, or to HTTP validation if the box is reachable on port 80.

Bought certs. If you pay a registrar for a cert because "that's how we did it in 2019", see whether your host can do ACME instead. A lot of paid CAs support ACME too, if you need a paid one for some reason.

Step 7: try the short certs early, on something that doesn't matter

You don't have to wait for February to find out what breaks. Two options:

  • Staging is already on 64-day certs. Point a throwaway subdomain at a test box, issue with --staging, and watch it over a couple of weeks.
  • Or opt one low-stakes production name into 45-day certs now. In recent certbot that's --preferred-profile tlsserver, which falls back to the default profile if the profile ever disappears. --required-profile fails instead, which you probably don't want on a real site.

If your setup survives 45-day certs, February is a non-event.

The one-hour version

If you only do part of this:

  1. Find what renews each cert, and write it down.
  2. Grep for 60, 80, 83, --force-renewal and renew_before_expiry. Upgrade old certbot and acme.sh.
  3. Make sure a successful renewal reloads whatever serves the cert.
  4. Add the outside check on every hostname, including the webhook host, alerting at 14 days, with a heartbeat on the check.
  5. Run crt.sh once to find hostnames you forgot.

Most of the time nothing is wrong. But "the cert expired" outages are almost always on a box someone set up once and stopped thinking about, and February takes away a lot of the slack those boxes have been living on.

What renews the certs on your server right now, and do you actually know what day it fires? And if anyone has already moved a real site to the 45-day tlsserver profile, did anything break?

  • If your "automation" is a cron line with --force-renewal on a fixed calendar, replace it with the plain certbot renew running twice a day. Certbot's docs recommend exactly that and say it's safe to run as often as you like, since it does nothing until a cert is due.

Step 3: renewal isn't deployment

This one gets people even with perfect timing. Certbot renews the file on disk. Nginx keeps serving the old cert from memory until it reloads. If nothing reloads it, the new cert sits there unused and the old one expires right on schedule.

With certbot, add a deploy hook. It only runs after a successful renewal:

sudo tee /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/reload-nginx.sh > /dev/null <<'HOOK'
#!/bin/sh
nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx
HOOK
sudo chmod +x /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/reload-nginx.sh

With acme.sh it's the --reloadcmd you pass when installing the cert. Their README flags it as IMPORTANT, and they're right.

Other places the new cert never reaches: a Docker image that copied the cert in at build time, a load balancer or CDN where you uploaded a cert by hand, a second server that gets the cert by rsync from the first one. On 90-day certs you might've caught that by accident. On 64-day certs, you get fewer accidents.

To test the renew-plus-hook path without touching real certs:

sudo certbot renew --dry-run --run-deploy-hooks

--dry-run talks to the staging server and doesn't save anything. Deploy hooks don't run during a dry run unless you add --run-deploy-hooks.

Step 4: check the certificate people actually get, from outside

Checking the file on disk tells you what certbot did. It doesn't tell you what browsers and Stripe see. I'd run something like this from a machine that isn't the server, once a day:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# check-certs.sh: fail if any cert you actually serve expires within DAYS days
DAYS=14
HOSTS="example.com www.example.com api.example.com status.example.com"

fail=0
for h in $HOSTS; do
  cert=$(echo | timeout 10 openssl s_client -connect "$h:443" -servername "$h" 2>/dev/null)
  end=$(echo "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -enddate 2>/dev/null | cut -d= -f2)
  if [ -z "$end" ]; then
    echo "FAIL $h: couldn't get a certificate"
    fail=1
  elif ! echo "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -checkend $((DAYS * 86400)) >/dev/null; then
    echo "FAIL $h: expires $end"
    fail=1
  else
    echo "ok   $h: expires $end"
  fi
done
exit $fail

-checkend takes seconds and exits 1 if the cert expires inside that window. -servername matters if more than one site lives on the same IP, otherwise you might be checking the wrong cert.

Pick the alert threshold for the new lifetimes. A lot of us have a "warn at 30 days left" rule from the 90-day era. On a 64-day cert renewed at about 2/3, a healthy cert hits 30 days left around day 34, roughly 9 days before renewal even tries. So the alert fires on every healthy cert, you mute it, and then it can't help you when it matters. I'd use 14 days for 64-day certs and something like 7 to 10 once you're on 45-day ones.

Where the alert goes matters as much as the check. The SideHunt guide on monitoring a side project when you can't watch it all day splits alerts into "interrupt me now" and "tonight is fine". A cert with 14 days left is a tonight one. A cert with 2 days left, or a FAIL on the webhook host, is a now one.

And the check script is itself a cron job that can die quietly. If it stops running, "no alerts" looks exactly like "everything's fine". I wrote about heartbeat checks for the jobs a tiny SaaS runs. Same idea here: ping on success so you hear about it when the check itself stops.

Step 5: find the certs you forgot about

The hostnames list in that script is only as good as your memory. Certificate Transparency logs remember better. Every public cert gets logged, so you can see every name anyone got a cert for on your domain:

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=example.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u

crt.sh is free and kind of slow, and sometimes it just returns a 502. Retry in a minute. What usually turns up: an old staging. subdomain still pointing at a box, status. on some service you set up once, a mail. cert on the mail server, a customer's custom domain. Anything still live goes into HOSTS. Anything dead, delete the DNS record so it stops being a thing.

While you're thinking about expiry dates, the domain itself expires too, and a cert check won't catch that one. The IndieHunt guide on protecting a small SaaS from account lockouts covers registrar lock, auto-renew and the "renewal emails go to the domain that expired" trap.

Step 6: if anything still renews by hand, fix that now

Two cases I'd look for:

Manual DNS challenges. If you ran certbot certonly --manual with DNS and paste a TXT record each time, certbot's docs are clear that those certs won't renew automatically unless you add auth hook scripts. Today Let's Encrypt reuses a successful validation for 30 days. From February 2027 that's 10 days, and on the 45-day schedule in 2028 it's 7 hours. So basically every renewal will need a fresh challenge. Move to a DNS plugin for your DNS provider, or to HTTP validation if the box is reachable on port 80.

Bought certs. If you pay a registrar for a cert because "that's how we did it in 2019", see whether your host can do ACME instead. A lot of paid CAs support ACME too, if you need a paid one for some reason.

Step 7: try the short certs early, on something that doesn't matter

You don't have to wait for February to find out what breaks. Two options:

  • Staging is already on 64-day certs. Point a throwaway subdomain at a test box, issue with --staging, and watch it over a couple of weeks.
  • Or opt one low-stakes production name into 45-day certs now. In recent certbot that's --preferred-profile tlsserver, which falls back to the default profile if the profile ever disappears. --required-profile fails instead, which you probably don't want on a real site.

If your setup survives 45-day certs, February is a non-event.

The one-hour version

If you only do part of this:

  1. Find what renews each cert, and write it down.
  2. Grep for 60, 80, 83, --force-renewal and renew_before_expiry. Upgrade old certbot and acme.sh.
  3. Make sure a successful renewal reloads whatever serves the cert.
  4. Add the outside check on every hostname, including the webhook host, alerting at 14 days, with a heartbeat on the check.
  5. Run crt.sh once to find hostnames you forgot.

Most of the time nothing is wrong. But "the cert expired" outages are almost always on a box someone set up once and stopped thinking about, and February takes away a lot of the slack those boxes have been living on.

What renews the certs on your server right now, and do you actually know what day it fires? And if anyone has already moved a real site to the 45-day tlsserver profile, did anything break?

title: Modeling a Real Org Chart in Toronto: Group, Division, Department, Team
summary:
A manufacturing group headquartered in Toronto, with a logistics division in Vancouver and a finance department that reports into both the division and a shared-services group at head office, is not an edge case. It is the normal shape of a mid-sized Canadian company. Most software tooling, though, still models access as a flat list of roles: admin, developer, viewer. That works for a ten-person startup. It falls apart the moment someone asks: who is allowed to approve a production release for the Vancouver warehouse system, and does that approval also need sign-off from the group's security lead in Toronto?

This is not a people-management question. It is an architecture question, and it belongs in the same conversation as authentication and data access, because an org chart that is wrong in software produces wrong approvals in production.

The org chart is a graph, not a tree

Group, division, department, team looks like strict nesting on a slide deck. In practice it rarely is. A QA lead might sit inside one department for reporting purposes but be the designated approver for releases across three teams. A plant manager in a Montreal facility might hold an operational role in the manufacturing division and a compliance role in a group-wide safety committee. Modeling this as a single-parent tree forces you to either duplicate the person across branches or flatten their permissions down to the lowest common denominator — usually the wrong one.

Corporate AI 365 treats the org chart as a real hierarchy with multi-hat roles: a person can hold distinct permission sets at different nodes simultaneously, and those permission sets are composable rather than bundled. There are 41 discrete permissions, not three role templates. That granularity exists specifically so that who can file a problem report, who can see the diagnosis, and who can approve the fix into production can be three different answers at three different nodes of the same hierarchy, without anyone being handed more access than their actual job requires.

Why the shape determines who can approve what

The product's delivery pipeline is Developer → QA → approval → production, implemented as real git branches and pull requests on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps. Each gate in that pipeline is a permission, and each transition is an audit record. The useful question in a security review is not whether that pipeline exists — most CI setups have something similar — but who is structurally allowed to sit at each gate, and whether that mapping survives the complexity of a real company.

Bind the approval gate to a department node and a national retailer's Toronto head office can require that only someone with release authority in that department — not just anyone with a developer badge — can push to production for a given system. Bind it to a division and you get regional autonomy: the Vancouver logistics team ships on its own cadence without waiting on Toronto, while the group retains visibility through the Manager console. This is the practical payoff of modeling the chart honestly: the governance gates mean something, because they're attached to the actual structure of who answers to whom, not to a generic role label.

Reporting problems without routing them through scarce senior engineers

Production downtime is expensive at any scale — industry estimates (ITIC) put the median cost for large enterprises at roughly US$9,000 per minute — and the usual bottleneck isn't willingness to fix things, it's finding someone senior enough to diagnose the root cause fast. That person is increasingly hard to find. Surveys across other markets report skills gaps as high as 90% of organizations in the Gulf and 57% of firms in Europe unable to find qualified developers; Canadian engineering leaders describe the same structural pressure anecdotally, even without a single national figure to cite. A lean IT team in Winnipeg or Halifax feels this as directly as one in Toronto.

This is where the org chart becomes operationally useful rather than administrative. The Employee support portal lets anyone in the company — a warehouse supervisor, an accounts clerk, a plant operator — file a problem report in plain language, no ticket taxonomy required. The hierarchy then routes that report to the right team automatically, because the system already knows which department owns which codebase. The AI reads the team's actual source code and scripted schema, proposes a root cause down to file, class, or line with a confidence score, and that diagnosis is cached against a hash of the issue text, the code snapshot, and the model — so a junior developer reviewing it a day later sees the same answer a senior one would have. That reproducibility is what lets a smaller team run production support without a bench of specialists standing by.

Worth stating plainly, because it matters in a review: none of this requires the AI to touch a live database. It reasons over source code and a scripted schema export you control. If the diagnosis genuinely needs live data, it writes a read-only query for your own developer to run — the result never comes back to us. The org hierarchy, the permissions, and the approval trail live entirely within your connected repository and your directory; verified domain join by DNS and SSO with Microsoft, Google, or GitHub mean the structure is yours, not something we infer or store independently.

title: How GCP Service Accounts Work for Database Access Tools
summary:
If you've ever connected a third-party tool to a GCP project, you've run into the same ritual: create a service account, attach some roles, download a JSON key, paste it somewhere. Most DBAs do this on autopilot without stopping to think about what a service account actually is, which roles it really needs, and what happens if that JSON key leaks.

That's worth slowing down for. Service account permissions are one of the most common places database security goes quietly wrong — not through a sophisticated attack, but through a service account granted far more than it needed, because "Editor" was faster to click than figuring out the right role.

TL;DR

A GCP service account's permissions come entirely from the IAM roles you attach — there's no implicit access beyond that. For a tool that only needs to discover Cloud SQL and Cloud Spanner instances, roles/cloudsql.viewer and roles/spanner.viewer are the only roles needed. 1DataCloud connects to GCP using exactly those two roles. Try it free →

What a GCP Service Account Actually Is

A service account is an identity — not a human one. It's what applications, scripts, and third-party tools use to authenticate to Google Cloud APIs, the way your own Google account authenticates you in the GCP Console.

The part that matters: a service account's permissions come entirely from the IAM roles you attach to it. There's no default level of access. A brand-new service account with no roles can do nothing.

Download its JSON key, and you're holding long-lived credentials for that identity. Anyone with that file can authenticate as the service account and do whatever its roles allow — which is exactly why the roles attached matter so much.

The Roles That Actually Matter for Database Discovery

For a tool that only needs to discover and inspect database instances — not modify them — two predefined roles cover it:

roles/cloudsql.viewer — read-only visibility into Cloud SQL: instance names, regions, tiers, versions, status, configuration. No create, modify, delete, or data access.

roles/spanner.viewer — the equivalent for Cloud Spanner: instance and database metadata, no schema or data modification.

Both are scoped specifically to metadata visibility for their service. Neither touches Compute Engine, billing, IAM, or anything else in the project.

What not to grant

The common shortcut is attaching Editor or Owner because it "definitely includes" whatever narrower permission is needed. It does — along with the ability to modify or delete nearly everything else in the project. A leaked key tied to a viewer role exposes metadata. A leaked key tied to Editor exposes your entire GCP project.

How 1DataCloud Uses This

1DataCloud's GCP connection runs on exactly roles/cloudsql.viewer and roles/spanner.viewer — nothing broader. With just those two roles, it uses the GCP API to discover every Cloud SQL and Cloud Spanner instance across every project the service account can see, automatically. No project-by-project browsing, no permissions beyond what's needed to build that inventory.

Once an instance is connected for querying, its schema is read and mapped so Query1AI can turn plain-English questions into read-only SQL — but the discovery step itself never required write access to anything.

If that JSON key were ever exposed, the worst case is someone viewing your database inventory metadata — not modifying a database, not touching unrelated GCP services, not reaching billing. That's a very different incident than a leaked key with Editor attached.

Mistakes Worth Avoiding

  • One service account for everything. A single, broadly-scoped account shared across five tools means a compromise of any one is a compromise of all five.
  • Keys that never rotate. A JSON key doesn't expire on its own.
  • Using the default Compute Engine service account, which often carries broad project-level permissions by default, for a narrow task like discovery.
  • Project-level roles when a resource-level one exists — even when the project-wide version is more convenient to click through.

Summary

A GCP service account is only as risky as the roles attached to it. For database discovery, roles/cloudsql.viewer and roles/spanner.viewer grant exactly enough visibility to build an inventory — nothing more. 1DataCloud's own GCP connection runs on exactly those two roles.

title: `docker push` Works on AI Agents Now
summary:
docker push Works on AI Agents Now

Docker Agent is a docker CLI plugin that turns an AI agent into an OCI artifact. You define the agent in YAML, run it with docker agent run, then ship it with docker agent share push to any OCI-compatible registry, Docker Hub or GitHub Container Registry included. Anyone on the team can then run your agent with docker agent run myorg/agent:tag (Docker Agent docs). An OCI artifact is the registry packaging format container images already use; here it carries an agent config instead of a filesystem. Push, pull, sign, pin by digest: the same lifecycle a container image has, applied to agents.

I run a small agent on a VM myself: it reads a pitch board, writes a Docker post, and stages it for publishing every morning. Getting that thing reproducible on another machine is exactly the problem this tool attacks, so I read the repo and docs end to end. The pitch board lives in Obsidian, the runs land in a ledger, and the whole setup is YAML plus scripts. The moment an agent has a config file, it wants a package format.

The problem is real enough to have a name around teams I know: the snowflake agent. The system prompt lives in a note app, the tool list lives in a repo nobody can find, and the one person who understands the setup is on holiday. Sharing means pasting YAML into a chat window and hoping the receiver reassembles it correctly, keys and all. Docker's engineering team open-sourced their answer in docker/docker-agent. The tagline is direct: "Build, run, and share AI agents with a declarative YAML config, rich tool ecosystem, and multi-agent orchestration."

In this post:

  • What Docker Agent actually is
  • The smallest agent is ten lines
  • Two agents beat one
  • Push it like an image
  • Sign it, verify it
  • Compose teams out of the registry
  • Where this breaks down
  • FAQ

Key Takeaways

  • Docker Agent is an open-source Apache-2.0 docker CLI plugin (repo); Docker Desktop 4.63+ ships it pre-installed, so docker agent works out of the box.
  • An agent is a YAML file: model, description, instruction, optional toolsets. Multi-agent configs add coordinators, specialists, and handoffs.
  • docker agent share push ./agent.yaml ghcr.io/username/my-agent:v1.0 packages the agent as an OCI artifact; docker agent run myorg/agent:tag runs it straight from the registry (distribution docs).
  • --key signs on push and verifies on pull using a DSSE envelope over an in-toto statement, the same ecosystem cosign speaks. Pin digests (myorg/agent@sha256:...) when rollback protection matters.

What Docker Agent actually is

Strip the branding and Docker Agent is a builder and runtime for agents, written in Go, that plugs into the docker CLI you already have. The repo describes itself as the "AI Agent Builder and Runtime by Docker Engineering" (docker/docker-agent). It is unusually active for a young project: over eleven thousand commits, 4.6k stars, and a release cadence that produced v1.152.0 in late October 2026.

Installation is the part I appreciate most, because it is nothing:

  • Docker Desktop 4.63+: the CLI plugin is pre-installed. You type docker agent and it works.
  • Homebrew: brew install docker-agent, or symlink the binary into ~/.docker/cli-plugins/.
  • Binaries: grab one from GitHub Releases and symlink it the same way.

A rename happened along the way, which is why older posts call it by a different binary name: in March 2026 the maintainers changed the usage samples to the docker agent plugin form. If you find a tutorial referencing the old invocation, it is describing the same tool.

Providers are pluggable, which matters if you have opinions about where your tokens go. The README lists OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Mistral, xAI, and Docker Model Runner for local models, plus custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints. You need at least one API key set, or a local Model Runner endpoint, before anything interesting happens. The docs walk both paths (Set Up a Model).

The smallest agent is ten lines

The README's minimal example is the whole mental model:

agents:
  root:
    model: openai/gpt-5-mini
    description: A helpful AI assistant
    instruction: |
      You are a knowledgeable assistant that helps users with various tasks.
      Be helpful, accurate, and concise in your responses.
    toolsets:
      - type: mcp
        ref: docker:duckduckgo

Run it with docker agent run agent.yaml. That is an agent: a model, a description the runtime shows when routing work, an instruction that is the system prompt, and toolsets. The mcp toolset type references any Model Context Protocol server, and the docker:duckduckgo ref is a catalog shorthand for DuckDuckGo search. The examples directory in the repo is a catalog of working configs. It is meant to be read as documentation, not just copied: the examples README groups them by the feature they showcase, from bare-minimum agents to remote MCP with OAuth.

Two details from the run command are worth knowing before your config grows. The -a flag picks a specific agent from a multi-agent file, and --exec skips the terminal UI for scripting. There is also docker agent new for generating a config interactively instead of writing YAML by hand.

Two agents beat one

Single agents hit a wall fast: the model juggles planning, searching, and writing in one context window, and quality slides as the task grows. Docker Agent's answer is multi-agent configuration, documented in detail on the multi-agent concepts page. A coordinator holds the goal; specialists hold the skills.

There are two shapes, and picking between them is the first real design decision:

Pattern What it does Session shape Tool
Delegation (sub_agents) Parent sends a task to a specialist, blocks, collects the result Child runs in its own sub-session with a clean task description transfer_task
Handoff (handoffs) The active agent switches; conversation continues Same session, full history visible to the next agent handoff

Delegation suits a coordinator that fans work out and synthesizes answers. Handoffs suit pipelines where the conversation itself moves down a chain, and they can form cycles: researcher to summarizer and back to root. The docs are explicit that you can mix both in one config, and that transfer_task is always auto-approved, so delegation does not generate permission prompts mid-run.

title: How Can Developers Add Dark Web Monitoring to Their Workflow?
summary:
Developers spend a lot of time protecting code, servers, and pipelines. Far less time goes into checking what’s already leaked outside those systems. Stolen logins, breach data, and exposed company details can sit on the dark web for months, and none of your logs will show it.

The fix isn’t complicated. You add an outside in check to your workflow, so leaked credentials get flagged before someone tries them. This post covers what to monitor, where it fits in your process, and how CyberDeleteme can help you get started without a big setup.

Why Do Leaked Credentials Slip Past Your Stack?

Because the leak doesn’t happen inside your stack. A user reuses a password on a third party site, that site gets breached, and the credentials end up in a dump. Your app never sees the breach, but the attacker can still try the login on your service.

Another source is infostealer data. Stealer logs hold credentials, financial details, and system information, and they’re often traded on the dark web. An employee’s infected device can leak a company login without touching your infrastructure at all.

What Should You Actually Monitor?

Start with three things. First, employee and service account emails. Second, your company domain. Third, anything tied to high access roles, like admins and finance staff. These carry the most risk if a credential leaks.

CyberDeleteme covers these with a few focused tools. The OneSearch Email Scan checks the dark web for breaches, leaks, credentials, and stealer logs. title: Choosing a Self-Hosted Jira Alternative: A Migration-Focused Decision Guide
summary:
Replacing Jira can disrupt more than ticket tracking: projects often depend on years of history, established workflows, and reporting routines. A self-hosted alternative also needs to fit your environment without forcing a team to rebuild everything at once.

This guide compares seven options using four practical criteria: self-hosting fit, project and agile coverage, workflow and reporting flexibility, and migration effort. The right choice depends on which of those constraints matters most to your team.

Comparison table

Redmine Teams seeking a self-hosted issue tracker with configurable project workflows. Self-hosted Not yet Free, open source Issue tracking, projects, and configurable fields and workflows. Yes
Taiga Agile teams managing backlogs, tasks, and iterative work in a self-hosted tool. Self-hosted Not yet Free and paid options Agile boards and backlog management. Yes
Tuleap Teams combining agile planning with software delivery and project traceability. Self-hosted API / MCP Free and paid editions Agile project management with traceability across development work. Yes

How to evaluate the options

Use the same checks for each candidate so the comparison reflects your actual work, not just feature lists:

  • Deployment fit: Confirm that the product can run in the environment your organization requires and support the work Jira handles today.
  • Project and agile coverage: Compare issue and task tracking, project plans, backlogs, sprints, and boards. A team managing both sprint work and a longer project plan needs more than ticket capture.
  • Workflow and reporting: Check whether teams can represent their work stages and produce the views they use to communicate progress and make decisions.
  • Migration effort: List the projects, issue types, fields, users, sprint data, workflow rules, reports, and dashboards that must be addressed. ONES.com’s migration guide describes loading a backup, selecting a target team and project, parsing data, mapping issue types, fields, and users, and confirming the migration. Its migration scope includes Jira sprints and workflow statuses and transitions; it also identifies elements that need separate planning.

Shortlist by requirement

  1. ONES.com: Start here if the decision includes migrating Jira project data and preserving supported sprints and workflow transitions. Its documented flow includes explicit mapping steps.
  2. Jira Data Center: Consider it when keeping Jira’s existing project and agile workflows in a self-managed environment is the priority.
  3. GitLab: A fit when issue planning should stay close to repository-based development and CI/CD work.
  4. Redmine: Consider it for self-hosted issue tracking with configurable project workflows, if its core feature set matches your needs.
  5. Taiga: A fit when backlog and Scrum or Kanban board execution are the central requirements.
  6. Tuleap: Consider it when agile planning and traceability across software development work matter most.
  7. Trac: A lightweight option for teams focused on self-hosted ticket tracking alongside code and documentation.

Tool reviews

ONES.com

Product Overview

ONES.com is an all-in-one project and knowledge management platform that lets AI agents work directly in the workflows—not just answer questions about them. For a self-hosted Jira replacement, ONES.com pairs on-premises deployment with migration tooling and project-delivery capabilities, making it a fit for teams that need to preserve project history and continue coordinating requirements, issues, and agile work in a controlled environment.

Why It Was Selected

ONES.com stands out when “comprehensive” means both broad delivery coverage and a defined path for transferring Jira projects. In its documented on-premises migration flow, an administrator loads a Jira backup, chooses the target team and project, parses the data, maps issue types, fields, and users, then confirms and runs the migration. The migration scope includes sprints and workflow statuses and transitions, so teams can carry key planning and process structures into the replacement rather than rebuilding everything from scratch. See the migration guide and migration data scope.

That combination addresses two decisive selection needs: moving existing Jira work with a planned mapping process, and continuing delivery across requirements, backlogs, sprints, releases, and project plans. For example, an administrator can map a team’s issue types and users during migration; afterward, the delivery team can organize work into a backlog and sprint and track the release. The practical value is continuity from transferred project data into ongoing execution.

Core Capabilities

  • Pain: A Jira replacement must keep project records associated with the right destination. Capability: Administrators select a target team and project before parsing and migrating a backup. Result: Imported work has a defined project destination.
  • Pain: Different teams use distinct issue types and fields. Capability: The migration flow maps Jira issue types and fields to ONES.com. Result: Teams can align transferred records with their target project structure.
  • Pain: User references need to remain meaningful after transfer. Capability: Administrators set an email suffix and map users during migration. Result: The migration process includes an explicit user-mapping step.
  • Pain: Agile teams need to resume planned work, not just view historical tickets. Capability: The migration scope supports Jira sprints. Result: Sprint information can travel with the migrated project.
  • Pain: Teams rely on defined workflow paths to manage issue progress. Capability: Migration supports workflow statuses and transitions. Result: Key status changes and movement between statuses can carry into the replacement.
  • Pain: Teams need a route from incoming work to an executable iteration. Capability: ONES.com supports backlogs, tasks, bugs, and sprints. Result: Teams can organize delivery work and plan it into sprint execution.
  • Pain: A release plan needs more than a list of issues. Capability: ONES.com supports Agile epics and roadmaps, releases, milestones, and deliverables. Result: Teams can connect work planning with release and milestone tracking.
  • Pain: Project leads need to coordinate schedule and progress across planned work. Capability: ONES.com supports Gantt planning alongside project tracking. Result: Teams can view delivery plans and track work within the same project environment.

Pros

  • Self-hosted deployment aligns with teams that need project management within a controlled environment.
  • The migration flow makes project, field, issue-type, and user mapping explicit before execution.
  • Support for sprints and workflow statuses and transitions connects migration fit to ongoing agile execution.
  • Delivery spans backlog and sprint work through roadmaps, releases, milestones, and Gantt planning.

Cons

  • Migration planning should account for the scope of what transfers: the documented Jira migration scope does not include workflow triggers, conditions, validators, or post-functions, and Jira reports and dashboards are not supported for migration.
  • The documented on-premises migration guide recommends ONES version 6.100.6 or later, so version planning is part of the migration setup.

Pricing

ONES On-Premises provides a 30-day free trial for up to 20 users. Paid plans use annual tiered per-seat pricing, with a 100-user minimum. See ONES.com Pricing.

Best For

ONES.com is best for organizations replacing Jira that want self-hosted project management, broad agile and delivery planning, and a structured migration path. It is especially relevant when administrators need to map existing Jira projects and users while teams need to carry sprint and workflow structures into day-to-day backlog, release, and milestone planning.

Jira Data Center

Jira Data Center is Atlassian’s self-managed Jira option and a useful incumbent benchmark. Teams can retain Jira’s project and issue model, configurable workflows, and agile boards. For example, a team can track an item through review, development, and release while using a board to show its current stage.

Advantages: It can preserve established Jira workflows and routines, supports configurable workflows and Scrum and Kanban boards, and runs in an environment managed by the organization.

Limitations: Complex workflow configurations and app dependencies can make upgrades and administration more involved. A move to another platform may require mapping fields, workflow states, permissions, reports, and app-specific data—not simply copying tickets. Teams should inventory their connected tools and reporting needs before choosing a replacement.

Pricing: Commercial licensing depends on the licensed edition and user tier. Marketplace apps may add costs, so compare the full annual subscription and app spend for the deployment in scope.

Best fit: Organizations already running Jira in a self-managed environment that prioritize continuity. It is less suited to teams whose aim is to replace Jira rather than retain its core model.

GitLab

GitLab combines software development tooling with a self-managed option and built-in issue tracking. Teams can associate a feature or defect issue with code changes and CI/CD activity, keeping planning and delivery progress together.

Advantages: Issues, planning, code collaboration, and CI/CD can share a development workflow. Boards, labels, milestones, and epics help teams organize work, while self-managed deployment supports control over where the platform runs.

Limitations: Its center of gravity is software development, so teams seeking broad cross-functional project management may find it less aligned with their needs. Jira configurations relying on specialized workflows, fields, or reports may need redesign rather than direct transfer. Capabilities also depend on the selected tier.

Pricing: GitLab offers tiered plans, including a self-managed option; pricing and capabilities depend on the selected tier and deployment.

Best fit: Software teams that want issues, agile planning, code changes, and CI/CD status connected in a self-managed development workflow.

Redmine

Redmine is an open-source, self-hosted project management and issue-tracking application. Teams can create projects, assign and prioritize issues, track status, log time, and relate issues to repositories and project versions.

Advantages: It gives organizations control over the hosting environment and provides issue tracking, project organization, time logging, roles, and configurable fields and workflows. For example, a team can assign a defect, log effort, and associate it with a project version.

Limitations: Its built-in agile planning and project-portfolio capabilities are narrower than those of platforms with a broader native toolkit. Advanced workflows, reporting, and team-specific processes may require configuration or extensions, adding maintenance work. Jira projects, fields, workflows, and historical records need a migration plan.

Pricing: Redmine is open-source software. Infrastructure and administration still have operating costs, which depend on how it is deployed and maintained.

Best fit: Teams that prioritize self-hosting and issue tracking and can keep project processes relatively straightforward. It is a less direct fit when comprehensive built-in agile planning, reporting, and workflow customization are requirements.

Taiga

Taiga is a self-hostable project-management tool focused on Scrum and Kanban. Teams can collect work in a backlog, select items for an iteration, and track progress on a board, or use a Kanban flow for continuous work.

Advantages: Self-hosting suits teams that need to run their project tool in their own environment. Scrum and Kanban offer familiar ways to plan and track agile work, and the focused model can keep backlog and board coordination straightforward.

Limitations: Its agile focus is narrower than a broad project-management suite. Teams with Jira-specific workflows or reporting requirements may need to adapt their processes, and a board-centered match does not establish that project structures and workflow behavior will transfer easily.

Pricing: Taiga offers self-hosted deployment. Check the current official pricing and licensing terms for the edition and support options you plan to use.

Best fit: Teams whose core requirement is self-hosted Scrum or Kanban planning. Before moving a larger Jira estate, compare reporting and workflow needs and map a representative project.

Tuleap

Tuleap is a self-hosted application lifecycle management platform for coordinating project planning and software-development work. Its engineering-oriented scope makes it a candidate for teams looking beyond basic issue tracking.

Advantages: Self-hosting gives organizations control over where the system runs, and its application lifecycle management focus aligns with software teams coordinating project and development work.

Limitations: Its engineering scope may be less aligned with teams seeking an extensive traditional project-management suite across nontechnical departments. Migration fit depends on how existing Jira structures and workflows map to the intended setup. Assess representative projects and compare required reporting and workflow behavior rather than assuming a direct match.

Pricing: Pricing depends on deployment and licensing arrangement; check Tuleap’s current pricing information for applicable terms.

Best fit: Software teams prioritizing self-hosting and an application lifecycle management environment. Teams with broad cross-functional requirements should assess its scope and test their Jira workflows before planning a transition.

Trac

Trac is a self-hosted system built around tickets, a wiki, and version-control browsing. A developer can record a defect as a ticket, link it to a code change, and keep technical notes in the project wiki.

Advantages: Tickets, wiki pages, and repository browsing place issue and development context together. Milestones and ticket queries provide a lightweight planning foundation, and plugins can extend the core system.

Limitations: Built-in planning and agile tooling are narrower than a comprehensive project-management suite. Advanced workflows or reporting may require plugins and additional administration; plugins also bring setup, compatibility, and maintenance work. Jira project data and workflows require deliberate migration planning, and the interface and administration model may feel dated compared with newer tools.

Pricing: Trac is open-source software with no license fee. Budget for infrastructure, installation, administration, and any plugin maintenance.

Best fit: Teams prioritizing self-hosted ticket tracking tied to code and documentation. It is a more limited fit when the requirement is broad, built-in agile execution, customizable workflows, and rich reporting.

Choosing based on your constraints

Start with the Jira work you cannot afford to disrupt: project history, sprint planning, custom workflows, connected tools, or reporting. Then test candidates against those requirements rather than treating self-hosting as proof of migration compatibility.

If migration is central, inventory a representative project: issue types, fields, users, sprints, workflow statuses and transitions, reports, and dashboards. Compare that inventory with the destination’s documented migration scope and identify any work that must be rebuilt or handled separately.

If agile execution is the main concern, walk through the team’s actual backlog, sprint, and board routine. If process control is more important, test whether workflow stages and reporting views match how teams route and review work.

Conditional recommendation

ONES.com is a reasonable first option to evaluate when you need self-hosted project management and a documented path for mapping Jira data, including supported sprint and workflow elements. It is not a complete migration of every Jira workflow or reporting component, so account for the documented exclusions.

Choose Jira Data Center when retaining Jira itself is the priority. Consider GitLab, Redmine, Taiga, Tuleap, or Trac when their particular development, issue-tracking, or agile workflow better matches your scope—and accept the associated trade-offs in breadth, customization, or migration work.

FAQs

Which self-hosted Jira alternative should I evaluate first when migration matters?

ONES.com is worth evaluating when you want a documented migration flow. Administrators load a backup, select a target team and project, map project data and users, and confirm the migration. Check the documented scope before planning around specific Jira data.

Can Jira sprints and workflows transfer to ONES.com?

The documented migration scope supports Jira project sprints and workflow statuses and transitions. Workflow triggers, conditions, validators, post-functions, reports, and dashboards are not included in that scope.

How should I compare project and agile capabilities?

Use a real team routine: issue and task tracking, backlog grooming, sprint planning, board updates, and the views used to review progress. Check whether each tool supports the work without relying on unverified assumptions about migration.

What should I check before moving Jira projects?

Inventory projects, issue types, fields, users, sprints, workflow stages and transitions, reports, and dashboards. Use that list to plan mappings, identify unsupported elements, and estimate follow-up work.
