  • Pain: Project leads need to coordinate schedule and progress across planned work. Capability: ONES.com supports Gantt planning alongside project tracking. Result: Teams can view delivery plans and track work within the same project environment.

Pros

  • Self-hosted deployment aligns with teams that need project management within a controlled environment.
  • The migration flow makes project, field, issue-type, and user mapping explicit before execution.
  • Support for sprints and workflow statuses and transitions connects migration fit to ongoing agile execution.
  • Delivery spans backlog and sprint work through roadmaps, releases, milestones, and Gantt planning.

Cons

  • Migration planning should account for the scope of what transfers: the documented Jira migration scope does not include workflow triggers, conditions, validators, or post-functions, and Jira reports and dashboards are not supported for migration.
  • The documented on-premises migration guide recommends ONES version 6.100.6 or later, so version planning is part of the migration setup.

Pricing

ONES On-Premises provides a 30-day free trial for up to 20 users. Paid plans use annual tiered per-seat pricing, with a 100-user minimum. See ONES.com Pricing.

Best For

ONES.com is best for organizations replacing Jira that want self-hosted project management, broad agile and delivery planning, and a structured migration path. It is especially relevant when administrators need to map existing Jira projects and users while teams need to carry sprint and workflow structures into day-to-day backlog, release, and milestone planning.

Jira Data Center

Jira Data Center is Atlassian’s self-managed Jira option and a useful incumbent benchmark. Teams can retain Jira’s project and issue model, configurable workflows, and agile boards. For example, a team can track an item through review, development, and release while using a board to show its current stage.

Advantages: It can preserve established Jira workflows and routines, supports configurable workflows and Scrum and Kanban boards, and runs in an environment managed by the organization.

Limitations: Complex workflow configurations and app dependencies can make upgrades and administration more involved. A move to another platform may require mapping fields, workflow states, permissions, reports, and app-specific data—not simply copying tickets. Teams should inventory their connected tools and reporting needs before choosing a replacement.

Pricing: Commercial licensing depends on the licensed edition and user tier. Marketplace apps may add costs, so compare the full annual subscription and app spend for the deployment in scope.

Best fit: Organizations already running Jira in a self-managed environment that prioritize continuity. It is less suited to teams whose aim is to replace Jira rather than retain its core model.

GitLab

GitLab combines software development tooling with a self-managed option and built-in issue tracking. Teams can associate a feature or defect issue with code changes and CI/CD activity, keeping planning and delivery progress together.

Advantages: Issues, planning, code collaboration, and CI/CD can share a development workflow. Boards, labels, milestones, and epics help teams organize work, while self-managed deployment supports control over where the platform runs.

Limitations: Its center of gravity is software development, so teams seeking broad cross-functional project management may find it less aligned with their needs. Jira configurations relying on specialized workflows, fields, or reports may need redesign rather than direct transfer. Capabilities also depend on the selected tier.

Pricing: GitLab offers tiered plans, including a self-managed option; pricing and capabilities depend on the selected tier and deployment.

Best fit: Software teams that want issues, agile planning, code changes, and CI/CD status connected in a self-managed development workflow.

Redmine

Redmine is an open-source, self-hosted project management and issue-tracking application. Teams can create projects, assign and prioritize issues, track status, log time, and relate issues to repositories and project versions.

Advantages: It gives organizations control over the hosting environment and provides issue tracking, project organization, time logging, roles, and configurable fields and workflows. For example, a team can assign a defect, log effort, and associate it with a project version.

Limitations: Its built-in agile planning and project-portfolio capabilities are narrower than those of platforms with a broader native toolkit. Advanced workflows, reporting, and team-specific processes may require configuration or extensions, adding maintenance work. Jira projects, fields, workflows, and historical records need a migration plan.

Pricing: Redmine is open-source software. Infrastructure and administration still have operating costs, which depend on how it is deployed and maintained.

Best fit: Teams that prioritize self-hosting and issue tracking and can keep project processes relatively straightforward. It is a less direct fit when comprehensive built-in agile planning, reporting, and workflow customization are requirements.

Taiga

Taiga is a self-hostable project-management tool focused on Scrum and Kanban. Teams can collect work in a backlog, select items for an iteration, and track progress on a board, or use a Kanban flow for continuous work.

Advantages: Self-hosting suits teams that need to run their project tool in their own environment. Scrum and Kanban offer familiar ways to plan and track agile work, and the focused model can keep backlog and board coordination straightforward.

Limitations: Its agile focus is narrower than a broad project-management suite. Teams with Jira-specific workflows or reporting requirements may need to adapt their processes, and a board-centered match does not establish that project structures and workflow behavior will transfer easily.

Pricing: Taiga offers self-hosted deployment. Check the current official pricing and licensing terms for the edition and support options you plan to use.

Best fit: Teams whose core requirement is self-hosted Scrum or Kanban planning. Before moving a larger Jira estate, compare reporting and workflow needs and map a representative project.

Tuleap

Tuleap is a self-hosted application lifecycle management platform for coordinating project planning and software-development work. Its engineering-oriented scope makes it a candidate for teams looking beyond basic issue tracking.

Advantages: Self-hosting gives organizations control over where the system runs, and its application lifecycle management focus aligns with software teams coordinating project and development work.

Limitations: Its engineering scope may be less aligned with teams seeking an extensive traditional project-management suite across nontechnical departments. Migration fit depends on how existing Jira structures and workflows map to the intended setup. Assess representative projects and compare required reporting and workflow behavior rather than assuming a direct match.

Pricing: Pricing depends on deployment and licensing arrangement; check Tuleap’s current pricing information for applicable terms.

Best fit: Software teams prioritizing self-hosting and an application lifecycle management environment. Teams with broad cross-functional requirements should assess its scope and test their Jira workflows before planning a transition.

Trac

Trac is a self-hosted system built around tickets, a wiki, and version-control browsing. A developer can record a defect as a ticket, link it to a code change, and keep technical notes in the project wiki.

Advantages: Tickets, wiki pages, and repository browsing place issue and development context together. Milestones and ticket queries provide a lightweight planning foundation, and plugins can extend the core system.

Limitations: Built-in planning and agile tooling are narrower than a comprehensive project-management suite. Advanced workflows or reporting may require plugins and additional administration; plugins also bring setup, compatibility, and maintenance work. Jira project data and workflows require deliberate migration planning, and the interface and administration model may feel dated compared with newer tools.

Pricing: Trac is open-source software with no license fee. Budget for infrastructure, installation, administration, and any plugin maintenance.

Best fit: Teams prioritizing self-hosted ticket tracking tied to code and documentation. It is a more limited fit when the requirement is broad, built-in agile execution, customizable workflows, and rich reporting.

Choosing based on your constraints

Start with the Jira work you cannot afford to disrupt: project history, sprint planning, custom workflows, connected tools, or reporting. Then test candidates against those requirements rather than treating self-hosting as proof of migration compatibility.

If migration is central, inventory a representative project: issue types, fields, users, sprints, workflow statuses and transitions, reports, and dashboards. Compare that inventory with the destination’s documented migration scope and identify any work that must be rebuilt or handled separately.

If agile execution is the main concern, walk through the team’s actual backlog, sprint, and board routine. If process control is more important, test whether workflow stages and reporting views match how teams route and review work.

Conditional recommendation

ONES.com is a reasonable first option to evaluate when you need self-hosted project management and a documented path for mapping Jira data, including supported sprint and workflow elements. It is not a complete migration of every Jira workflow or reporting component, so account for the documented exclusions.

Choose Jira Data Center when retaining Jira itself is the priority. Consider GitLab, Redmine, Taiga, Tuleap, or Trac when their particular development, issue-tracking, or agile workflow better matches your scope—and accept the associated trade-offs in breadth, customization, or migration work.

FAQs

Which self-hosted Jira alternative should I evaluate first when migration matters?

ONES.com is worth evaluating when you want a documented migration flow. Administrators load a backup, select a target team and project, map project data and users, and confirm the migration. Check the documented scope before planning around specific Jira data.

Can Jira sprints and workflows transfer to ONES.com?

The documented migration scope supports Jira project sprints and workflow statuses and transitions. Workflow triggers, conditions, validators, post-functions, reports, and dashboards are not included in that scope.

How should I compare project and agile capabilities?

Use a real team routine: issue and task tracking, backlog grooming, sprint planning, board updates, and the views used to review progress. Check whether each tool supports the work without relying on unverified assumptions about migration.

What should I check before moving Jira projects?

Inventory projects, issue types, fields, users, sprints, workflow stages and transitions, reports, and dashboards. Use that list to plan mappings, identify unsupported elements, and estimate follow-up work.

title: Workflow Retries Can Duplicate Business Actions: A 12-Case Replay-Safety Test
summary:
Workflow Retries Can Duplicate Business Actions: A 12-Case Replay-Safety Test

A workflow can fail after a destination has already accepted an action. That means the red failure badge does not prove that no invoice, message, CRM record, or booking was created. If the workflow retries the same step without a stable business identity and a way to check the destination, an ordinary recovery action can become a duplicate. The practical rule is simple: retry only when the failure is known to be before the side effect, or when the destination can safely deduplicate the same intended action. Treat a timeout after dispatch as unknown until you reconcile it.

For a readable baseline on automation design, see AI workflow automation explained. This article narrows the question to a specific operational decision: when should a low-code workflow replay a step that sends or creates something outside the automation platform? It gives you a small acceptance suite you can run in a sandbox before enabling retries in production.

The answer in one minute

Do not use “the run failed” as a retry rule. Use the point at which the failure happened. A validation error before a request leaves the workflow is different from a connection reset after the receiver commits the request. In the second case, the caller knows only that it did not receive an acknowledgement. It does not know whether the business action happened.

Before an externally visible write, assign one stable key to the underlying business intent. Persist the key and a normalized request fingerprint. Send that same key to the receiver on every retry if the receiver supports idempotency. Store the receiver’s result before moving to later workflow steps. If the result is ambiguous and the receiver does not support idempotency, query by a durable business reference or send the item to a human reconciliation queue. Never “fix” uncertainty by generating a fresh key and sending again.

This approach is not a promise of exactly-once delivery. It is a practical way to make at-least-once delivery produce one business effect where the receiver cooperates, while exposing the cases where that is not possible. A workflow platform can resume nodes, save inputs, and schedule retries; it cannot atomically commit a local execution record and an unrelated remote system unless both systems share a transaction or an explicit deduplication contract.

Why the failed run can hide a successful action

Imagine a scenario that creates a quote in a CRM, sends an email, then writes a row to an internal sheet. The CRM returns a record ID. The email provider accepts the message. The sheet API then times out. The automation platform displays a failed execution because the final step did not complete. If an operator retries the entire scenario, all three actions may run again depending on the platform’s resume behavior. Even if the platform retries only the failed node, that node may have performed some work for earlier items in a batch before it stopped.

The ambiguity is a network fact, not a product defect. The receiver can commit a write and lose the response while it travels back. From the caller’s perspective, a timeout is consistent with at least two realities: the destination never received the request, or it committed the request but the acknowledgement did not arrive. A local log saying “timeout” cannot distinguish those realities by itself.

Three records are often confused. The automation execution ID identifies a run. A message or item ID identifies a piece of input. A business operation ID identifies one intended side effect, such as “send invoice reminder for invoice 742, reminder step 2.” Retries may create new execution IDs while still representing the same intended business action. Deduplicating only on execution ID therefore misses the duplicate. Deduplicating only on invoice ID may suppress a legitimate later reminder. The identity must be scoped to the intended effect.

This distinction also matters for batches. If a node processes 40 rows and fails after sending 13 messages, a retry may replay the node’s saved input, not magically know which 13 were accepted. A human may see a single failed run even though some recipients received a message. The unit of idempotency should therefore usually be one business effect per item, not one whole batch and not one whole run.

What the platforms actually say

The n8n execution documentation explains that completed node results are kept when retrying from saved execution state, but the failed node gets its saved input again and processes every item, including items it may have handled before it failed. Its own example warns that a node which sent some messages before failing can send those messages again. The same page says a retried sub-workflow starts again at its beginning, and that each retry is a new execution; retrying both the original and a failed retry can repeat work. These are important details to test against the version and configuration you actually run.

Make documents a different but related behavior. Its automatic retry documentation says automatic retries apply to certain incomplete execution causes, including rate-limit, connection, and module-timeout errors, and start again from the module that caused the error. It describes exponential-backoff scheduling and a limit on concurrent retries for a scenario. Other error types generally need manual resolution rather than being retried automatically. That is a useful control for transient availability, but a schedule and an error classification do not prove that an external write did not commit.

Neither product’s documentation should be generalized into “all retries replay the entire scenario” or “the platform always prevents duplicates.” The n8n page describes saved node state and the failed node’s saved inputs. Make describes incomplete executions and its selected retry policy. A platform, a particular module, a batch, an error handler, and a destination API can each change the result. Capture the exact configuration, then test the behavior you depend on.

Receiver behavior is another separate contract. Stripe’s idempotent request API is an example of a destination that accepts a client-supplied key and returns the stored result for subsequent requests using that key, subject to its documented behavior and retention. The key is meaningful because the receiver participates in deduplication. Adding a field named idempotency_key to a workflow payload does nothing if the receiving endpoint ignores it.

The decision table: retry, reconcile, or stop

Use this table when an operator or error handler must decide the next state. “Safe to retry” here means the business effect is known not to have occurred, or the destination’s deduplication contract makes the same request safe. It does not mean every transient error deserves another attempt.

Evidence at failure time What is known Default action Required control
Local validation fails before dispatch No external request was sent Correct input; retry after validation Preserve validation error and changed-input history
DNS or connection setup fails before an HTTP request can be sent Usually no application request reached the receiver, but check the client stack Retry within a bounded policy Backoff, attempt limit, confirm transport evidence
Receiver returns a documented rejection before commit The receiver says it did not accept the write Retry only if the response is transient Classify status; honor Retry-After; do not retry permanent validation errors
Receiver returns success and response is stored durably The action was accepted and its result is known Continue from the next step Persist external ID and result before resuming
Timeout or reset after dispatch; no receiver result The action may or may not have committed Reconcile; do not blind retry Reuse receiver key or query by a unique reference
Batch step partially succeeds and then fails Some items may have committed Replay per item only with dedupe Track each item’s operation key and result
Receiver has no idempotency key and no lookup by reference A duplicate cannot be excluded Stop for a person or accept explicit duplicate risk Manual resolution and auditable decision
Two retry paths are simultaneously available More than one actor may replay the same intent Select one retry owner Claim/lease and compare-and-set state transition

The table is deliberately conservative. If your transport can prove the request did not leave the client, you may classify that case as not dispatched. If it cannot prove that, use unknown. A broad “retry all 5xx” rule can be safe for some read-only operations and unsafe for a create endpoint. A status code describes the response received; it does not always define what happened before the response.

A small operation ledger

For every side-effecting item, keep a compact ledger keyed by a stable operation ID. A useful record contains the workflow or scenario identifier, business object identifier, action type, operation sequence, request fingerprint, status, attempt count, receiver request ID, returned object ID, timestamps, and a redacted failure class. Avoid copying secrets, full personal data, or entire message bodies into the ledger. It should be enough to locate the authoritative record and detect that a retry changed its meaning.

Four states are sufficient for a practical first version:

  • prepared: the workflow accepted a specific intent and persisted its identity before dispatch.
  • in_flight: a network call may have started; the external action must be assumed possible.
  • succeeded: a receiver response or reconciliation result is durably recorded.
  • unknown: available evidence cannot prove either success or failure.

You may also use failed for a known non-commit, such as a local schema rejection or a definitive receiver rejection whose contract says no write occurred. Do not use failed for every exception. If the HTTP client timed out waiting for a response, unknown is the honest state.

The state machine should be monotonic with respect to knowledge. A record can move from prepared to in_flight, and then to succeeded, failed, or unknown. Reconciliation can move unknown to succeeded or to a confirmed failed state. It should not silently turn unknown into “not sent” because a retry button was clicked. Store the operator and evidence behind a manual resolution.

The operation ID should be stable across replay of the same business intent and different for a new intent. One derivation might combine a tenant or workflow key, the destination record, an action name, and an explicit action sequence: tenant-8:invoice-742:reminder:2. If the action is an order creation, a stable checkout or request identifier may already exist. Avoid deriving the identity from mutable prose, current time, or a fresh random value generated during every retry. Conversely, avoid a key so broad that it merges two legitimate writes.

Store a fingerprint of the normalized request alongside the key. On replay, compare the new payload to the recorded fingerprint. If the same key arrives with a different recipient, amount, or action, return a conflict and require a new approved operation. This protects against key reuse bugs and unexpected data changes while a workflow is waiting for recovery.

The replay protocol

The workflow needs a clear boundary around the side effect. First validate the data and authorization. Then derive the operation ID from business identity. Persist a prepared row atomically, or load the existing row. If that row is already succeeded, return its saved result to downstream steps and do not call the destination. If it is unknown or in_flight, reconcile it or route it for review. Only a new, claimed prepared operation can be dispatched. When the receiver supports idempotency, pass the stable key and identical parameters. Finally, store the receiver result durably before allowing the next workflow step to depend on it.

That last ordering prevents a workflow from reaching a later stage while the only evidence of the write still exists in process memory. The sequence is not a distributed transaction. A process can still crash after the receiver commits and before the local ledger changes to succeeded. The ledger will then say in_flight, which is why recovery must reconcile or repeat with the same receiver key. A local success flag alone cannot close a remote crash window.

flowchart TD
  A[Validate business intent] --> B[Derive stable per-effect ID]
  B --> C[Persist or load operation row]
  C --> D{Recorded state?}
  D -->|Succeeded| E[Reuse stored result; skip write]
  D -->|Prepared and claimed| F[Dispatch with same receiver key]
  D -->|In flight or unknown| G[Query receiver or reconcile]
  G -->|Committed| H[Record success and result]
  G -->|Definitely not committed| F
  G -->|Still uncertain| I[Human queue; preserve unknown]
  F --> J{Response outcome?}
  J -->|Success| H
  J -->|Ambiguous timeout| I
  J -->|Definitive rejection| K[Record known failure]
  H --> E

A minimal receiver-side example

The strongest simple design is for the receiver to store the idempotency key in the same transaction as the business write. A workflow caller can then repeat the same request and receive the prior result. This illustrative TypeScript-like pseudocode assumes a database unique constraint and a request hash; it is not a drop-in library. The important point is the transaction boundary, not the syntax.

async function createInvoiceReminder(input: ReminderInput) {
  const key = input.operationId; // stable for this invoice + reminder sequence
  const requestHash = sha256(canonicalJson({
    invoiceId: input.invoiceId,
    recipientId: input.recipientId,
    reminderSequence: input.sequence,
  }));

  return db.transaction(async tx => {
    const prior = await tx.idempotency.findUnique({ key });
    if (prior) {
      if (prior.requestHash !== requestHash) {
        throw new ConflictError("same operation key, different request");
      }
      return prior.response;
    }

    const reminder = await tx.reminders.create({
      invoiceId: input.invoiceId,
      recipientId: input.recipientId,
      sequence: input.sequence,
    });
    const response = { reminderId: reminder.id, status: "queued" };
    await tx.idempotency.insert({ key, requestHash, response });
    return response;
  });
}

This design works only if the receiver owns both the action and the idempotency record in the same transactional store. If it inserts the deduplication row in one database and sends an email through an unrelated service, the same gap returns: the database transaction may commit while the email delivery remains uncertain. An outbox can make the intent durable and let a dispatcher retry, but the email provider or consumer still needs deduplication or reconciliation to make the externally visible effect idempotent.

Use a transactional outbox when a database write triggers another system

Suppose an order update and a message must both happen. Writing the order and making an HTTP request inside one workflow step cannot make the two systems atomic. A process can die between them. A transactional outbox changes the local part: the order update and an outbox event are committed in one database transaction. A separate dispatcher reads pending events, sends them, and marks them delivered. That avoids losing the intent after the database commit. It does not alone guarantee that the destination receives exactly one message. If the destination commits and its response is lost, the dispatcher can send again. Put the same operation ID on the event, and require destination deduplication or a reconciliation path.

When the destination is a database you control, an inbox table with a unique event key can suppress duplicate consumption. When the destination is an API you do not control, use its documented idempotency field if available and keep the key alive for longer than your possible retry window. If neither option exists, record the boundary and choose an explicit risk policy. “We use an outbox” is not an end-to-end delivery guarantee; it is one layer of the contract.

The twelve-case acceptance suite

The following cases are a proposed synthetic test matrix dated 26 October 2026. The sample size is 12 constructed scenarios, not 12 production incidents or measured outcomes. It is meant to expose behavior before a rollout. Replace the fixture names with one of your own write steps and run the test against a sandbox, including the exact platform and destination configuration you intend to deploy.

# Injected situation Expected ledger result Expected external effect Gate
1 Input validation rejects before dispatch failed with validation class None Correct input then create a new attempt under the same intent only if no request was sent
2 DNS lookup fails before the client can connect failed or known-not-dispatched None Bounded retry; confirm transport boundary in logs
3 Receiver returns a documented 429 before processing failed / retryable None for that request Respect Retry-After, same operation ID, finite retry budget
4 Receiver returns a permanent 400 validation rejection failed / non-retryable None if receiver contract says validation precedes commit Stop and surface changed-input review
5 Receiver commits, then response is dropped unknown until queried One action Repeat with same receiver key or reconcile by operation ID
6 Receiver returns success; workflow crashes before ledger result is saved in_flight on recovery One action Receiver query or same-key replay returns existing result
7 Receiver returns success and ledger persists, then later node fails succeeded One action Retry should reuse result and skip the write node
8 Batch of three items commits first two; third returns error Per-item states: two succeeded, one classified Two actions before recovery Replay the third only; never replay the whole batch without dedupe
9 Same operation key is replayed with identical payload succeeded or prior result One action total Return stored receiver result
10 Same key is replayed with a changed amount or recipient Conflict No new action Stop; require a new approved intent and key
11 Operator clicks retry on both original and retry execution One caller should win the claim One action total Compare-and-set or lease; second caller reuses or observes state
12 Receiver has no key and lookup returns no reliable result unknown Could be zero or one Human reconciliation; prohibit automatic blind replay

For each fixture, assert both sides of the boundary: the ledger and the destination. A test that checks only the workflow’s final status can miss a duplicated email. A test that counts destination records but ignores the workflow state can miss a lost action that never retries. Keep the expected result explicit for every case.

Record the platform name and version, workflow export or scenario blueprint hash, destination module and version, retry settings, batch size, error handler configuration, and test timestamp. For each fault, state exactly where it was injected: before connection, after request bytes were sent, after commit, or after the response arrived but before local persistence. “Simulate timeout” is not reproducible unless you identify the boundary.

For a new workflow, this can be a manual sandbox exercise. Create a receiver stub that logs operation IDs and can be configured to drop a response after recording a write. Run each fixture twice with the same business event. The expected total count for a deduplicated action is one. Then run the changed-payload fixture with the same key; it should fail closed. Do not use a live customer account or send real messages during the fault test.

A bounded retry policy that complements deduplication

Idempotency prevents a repeated request from creating another effect when the destination honors the contract. It does not make unlimited retries wise. Set a per-operation attempt cap and an overall time budget. Use exponential backoff with jitter for transient errors, honor server-provided retry delays, and stop retrying errors that cannot change on their own, such as invalid input or missing authorization. A retry should happen at one chosen layer, not independently in a node, a sub-workflow, a client SDK, and a queue consumer unless the combined behavior has been analyzed.

Google’s SRE chapter on addressing cascading failures explains how retries can add load during an overload and recommends randomized exponential backoff, bounded attempts, and a system-wide retry budget. Its examples are service-call failures, not a study of low-code workflow products, so apply the mechanism carefully: a process can create duplicates even at low traffic, while retry amplification is a separate availability risk. One fix does not solve the other.

A recent preprint, Retry Amplification in Distributed Systems, analyzes retry policies in open-source Python microservice projects and simulations. The authors report detected retry code in 23 of 200 projects, but explicitly describe that as a detection rate because their rules have false negatives. They also note their configuration sample is concentrated in a small number of repositories and the simulation uses a particular model. Treat its figures as evidence that retry behavior deserves system-level review, not as an estimate of how often your automation duplicates actions.

Failure modes that a button cannot solve

A fresh key on every retry. This turns retries into new requests from the receiver’s perspective. Generate and persist the key before the first attempt, then reuse it for the same business intent.

A key that lives only in workflow memory. A restarted process may lose the value and create another. Put it in a durable execution store or derive it deterministically from immutable business identifiers and persist the result.

The receiver silently ignores the key. A request field is not a deduplication guarantee. Verify the receiving API’s documentation, scope, parameter matching, concurrency behavior, and retention period. Stripe, for example, documents that keys can be pruned after a retention period; do not assume a key works forever.

A batch-level key for item-level writes. If a batch partially succeeds, retrying one key for the batch may either duplicate every item or suppress items that never ran. Prefer a distinct stable key for each intended external effect.

An incorrect “retryable” classification. A timeout after a write is ambiguous; a 400 is usually not repaired by waiting; a 429 may be safe to retry after the stated delay, but only if the destination’s contract says it rejected the operation. Model these as different states.

Multiple retry owners. If the automation platform, an error handler, a queue, and an operator all retry, the actual attempt count can exceed each local setting. Google SRE discusses how retries at multiple layers multiply load. Use one owner where practical, or a shared retry budget and a claim mechanism.

No reconciliation endpoint. If the remote API cannot accept an idempotency key or be queried by a business reference, an ambiguous request cannot be made safe by a workflow-only change. Route it for manual reconciliation, or redesign the integration around a receiver you control.

A successful run that did the wrong thing. A green status confirms that the configured path completed, not that the business outcome was correct. n8n notes that a retry is not available for a successful execution; running a copied workflow again can repeat downstream actions. Add output assertions and business-result checks rather than using replay as a correction tool.

A manual operator makes a second copy of the event. A recovery spreadsheet can itself create a duplicate if it does not carry the original operation ID. The operator interface should show the destination object ID, last known state, and the reason a retry is permitted.

An idempotency record expires too early. If the destination forgets a key before a delayed recovery occurs, a replay may be treated as new. Keep the local operation record and compare the oldest possible retry delay with receiver retention. When retention is short, reconcile first after expiry.

An update is mistaken for a create. “Append or create” is not replay-safe just because the destination is a database. Prefer a stable unique constraint, upsert keyed by business identity, or insert-on-conflict behavior. Verify that the update operation does not overwrite a later legitimate change with stale workflow input.

What to measure after release

Track the number of operations entering unknown, the age of the oldest unresolved operation, retries per business operation, receiver duplicate conflicts, actions recovered through idempotency keys, manual reconciliations, and the fraction of retries that end in a known result. Keep these measures separate from total workflow failure rate. A low failure rate can coexist with duplicate business effects, while a high retry count can exist without duplicates if the receiver deduplicates correctly.

Do not choose a universal threshold without a baseline. Start by recording the counts for a bounded observation window and splitting by destination, action type, and error class. An invoice creation and a read-only enrichment call should not share the same risk tolerance. If you set a page threshold, define who receives it, what action they take, and how the alert avoids revealing customer data.

For a recovery queue, include a direct link to the execution, stable operation ID, destination request or object ID if known, last attempt time, redacted error class, retry count, and next permitted action. Make the action labels unambiguous: “retry with same key,” “query destination,” “mark confirmed not committed,” or “escalate.” Avoid one generic “retry” button that hides the consequence.

Governance and business ownership

Replay safety is an operating rule, not only a developer preference. The business owner decides what counts as one action, which duplicates are unacceptable, and when a human must decide. The platform owner knows the execution semantics. The API owner confirms receiver guarantees. The operations team owns the unknown-outcome queue. If these responsibilities are split, write down who can change a retry setting and who can authorize a reissue after uncertainty.

Where this recommendation does not apply

For a pure read operation, repeating a request may be harmless, though it can still cost money, trigger rate limits, or return newer data. For a write that is naturally idempotent—such as setting a field to a fixed value under a stable record key—repeating may not create a duplicate, but stale input can still overwrite newer data. For a destination that gives a documented idempotency guarantee, same-key retry may be the best path within the guarantee’s scope and retention window. For a one-way notification with no receiver deduplication and no lookup, a human may be the only honest choice after an ambiguous timeout.

The word “exactly once” is often used too loosely. A queue may deliver at least once; an API may deduplicate a request key; a database transaction may make two local writes atomic; an operator process may reconcile unknown state. These are different guarantees. State the boundary: exactly one row in a particular database, one receiver-side action per retained key, or one workflow attempt in a platform. Do not transfer a narrow guarantee to the entire end-to-end business process.

The strongest design is not always worth building. If the action is low impact and easily reversible, a visible duplicate with a simple compensation path may be acceptable.   • [ ] Distinguish the run ID, input item ID, and business operation ID.
  • [ ] Define an operation key that survives restart and distinguishes legitimate repeated actions.
  • [ ] Persist the key and a normalized request fingerprint before the first dispatch.
  • [ ] Confirm from the receiving API’s documentation whether it honors an idempotency key, how it scopes keys, and how long it retains them.
  • [ ] Record a receiver request ID or returned object ID when available.

The release decision is therefore conditional. Workflow Retries Can Duplicate Business Actions: A 12-Case Replay-Safety Test

A workflow can fail after a destination has already accepted an action. That means the red failure badge does not prove that no invoice, message, CRM record, or booking was created. If the workflow retries the same step without a stable business identity and a way to check the destination, an ordinary recovery action can become a duplicate. The practical rule is simple: retry only when the failure is known to be before the side effect, or when the destination can safely deduplicate the same intended action. Treat a timeout after dispatch as unknown until you reconcile it.

For a readable baseline on automation design, see AI workflow automation explained. This article narrows the question to a specific operational decision: when should a low-code workflow replay a step that sends or creates something outside the automation platform? It gives you a small acceptance suite you can run in a sandbox before enabling retries in production.

The answer in one minute

Do not use “the run failed” as a retry rule. Use the point at which the failure happened. A validation error before a request leaves the workflow is different from a connection reset after the receiver commits the request. In the second case, the caller knows only that it did not receive an acknowledgement. It does not know whether the business action happened.

Before an externally visible write, assign one stable key to the underlying business intent. Persist the key and a normalized request fingerprint. Send that same key to the receiver on every retry if the receiver supports idempotency. Store the receiver’s result before moving to later workflow steps. If the result is ambiguous and the receiver does not support idempotency, query by a durable business reference or send the item to a human reconciliation queue. Never “fix” uncertainty by generating a fresh key and sending again.

This approach is not a promise of exactly-once delivery. It is a practical way to make at-least-once delivery produce one business effect where the receiver cooperates, while exposing the cases where that is not possible. A workflow platform can resume nodes, save inputs, and schedule retries; it cannot atomically commit a local execution record and an unrelated remote system unless both systems share a transaction or an explicit deduplication contract.

Why the failed run can hide a successful action

Imagine a scenario that creates a quote in a CRM, sends an email, then writes a row to an internal sheet. The CRM returns a record ID. The email provider accepts the message. The sheet API then times out. The automation platform displays a failed execution because the final step did not complete. If an operator retries the entire scenario, all three actions may run again depending on the platform’s resume behavior. Even if the platform retries only the failed node, that node may have performed some work for earlier items in a batch before it stopped.

The ambiguity is a network fact, not a product defect. The receiver can commit a write and lose the response while it travels back. From the caller’s perspective, a timeout is consistent with at least two realities: the destination never received the request, or it committed the request but the acknowledgement did not arrive. A local log saying “timeout” cannot distinguish those realities by itself.

Three records are often confused. The automation execution ID identifies a run. A message or item ID identifies a piece of input. A business operation ID identifies one intended side effect, such as “send invoice reminder for invoice 742, reminder step 2.” Retries may create new execution IDs while still representing the same intended business action. Deduplicating only on execution ID therefore misses the duplicate. Deduplicating only on invoice ID may suppress a legitimate later reminder. The identity must be scoped to the intended effect.

This distinction also matters for batches. If a node processes 40 rows and fails after sending 13 messages, a retry may replay the node’s saved input, not magically know which 13 were accepted. A human may see a single failed run even though some recipients received a message. The unit of idempotency should therefore usually be one business effect per item, not one whole batch and not one whole run.

What the platforms actually say

The n8n execution documentation explains that completed node results are kept when retrying from saved execution state, but the failed node gets its saved input again and processes every item, including items it may have handled before it failed. Its own example warns that a node which sent some messages before failing can send those messages again. The same page says a retried sub-workflow starts again at its beginning, and that each retry is a new execution; retrying both the original and a failed retry can repeat work. These are important details to test against the version and configuration you actually run.

Make documents a different but related behavior. Its automatic retry documentation says automatic retries apply to certain incomplete execution causes, including rate-limit, connection, and module-timeout errors, and start again from the module that caused the error. It describes exponential-backoff scheduling and a limit on concurrent retries for a scenario. Other error types generally need manual resolution rather than being retried automatically. That is a useful control for transient availability, but a schedule and an error classification do not prove that an external write did not commit.

Neither product’s documentation should be generalized into “all retries replay the entire scenario” or “the platform always prevents duplicates.” The n8n page describes saved node state and the failed node’s saved inputs. Make describes incomplete executions and its selected retry policy. A platform, a particular module, a batch, an error handler, and a destination API can each change the result. Capture the exact configuration, then test the behavior you depend on.

Receiver behavior is another separate contract. Stripe’s idempotent request API is an example of a destination that accepts a client-supplied key and returns the stored result for subsequent requests using that key, subject to its documented behavior and retention. The key is meaningful because the receiver participates in deduplication. Adding a field named idempotency_key to a workflow payload does nothing if the receiving endpoint ignores it.

The decision table: retry, reconcile, or stop

Use this table when an operator or error handler must decide the next state. “Safe to retry” here means the business effect is known not to have occurred, or the destination’s deduplication contract makes the same request safe. It does not mean every transient error deserves another attempt.

The table is deliberately conservative. If your transport can prove the request did not leave the client, you may classify that case as not dispatched. If it cannot prove that, use unknown. A broad “retry all 5xx” rule can be safe for some read-only operations and unsafe for a create endpoint. A status code describes the response received; it does not always define what happened before the response.

A small operation ledger

For every side-effecting item, keep a compact ledger keyed by a stable operation ID. A useful record contains the workflow or scenario identifier, business object identifier, action type, operation sequence, request fingerprint, status, attempt count, receiver request ID, returned object ID, timestamps, and a redacted failure class. Avoid copying secrets, full personal data, or entire message bodies into the ledger. It should be enough to locate the authoritative record and detect that a retry changed its meaning.

Four states are sufficient for a practical first version:

  • prepared: the workflow accepted a specific intent and persisted its identity before dispatch.
  • in_flight: a network call may have started; the external action must be assumed possible.
  • succeeded: a receiver response or reconciliation result is durably recorded.
  • unknown: available evidence cannot prove either success or failure.

You may also use failed for a known non-commit, such as a local schema rejection or a definitive receiver rejection whose contract says no write occurred. Do not use failed for every exception. If the HTTP client timed out waiting for a response, unknown is the honest state.

The state machine should be monotonic with respect to knowledge. A record can move from prepared to in_flight, and then to succeeded, failed, or unknown. Reconciliation can move unknown to succeeded or to a confirmed failed state. It should not silently turn unknown into “not sent” because a retry button was clicked. Store the operator and evidence behind a manual resolution.

The operation ID should be stable across replay of the same business intent and different for a new intent. One derivation might combine a tenant or workflow key, the destination record, an action name, and an explicit action sequence: tenant-8:invoice-742:reminder:2. If the action is an order creation, a stable checkout or request identifier may already exist. Avoid deriving the identity from mutable prose, current time, or a fresh random value generated during every retry. Conversely, avoid a key so broad that it merges two legitimate writes.

Store a fingerprint of the normalized request alongside the key. On replay, compare the new payload to the recorded fingerprint. If the same key arrives with a different recipient, amount, or action, return a conflict and require a new approved operation. This protects against key reuse bugs and unexpected data changes while a workflow is waiting for recovery.

The replay protocol

The workflow needs a clear boundary around the side effect. First validate the data and authorization. Then derive the operation ID from business identity. Persist a prepared row atomically, or load the existing row. If that row is already succeeded, return its saved result to downstream steps and do not call the destination. If it is unknown or in_flight, reconcile it or route it for review. Only a new, claimed prepared operation can be dispatched. When the receiver supports idempotency, pass the stable key and identical parameters. Finally, store the receiver result durably before allowing the next workflow step to depend on it.

That last ordering prevents a workflow from reaching a later stage while the only evidence of the write still exists in process memory. The sequence is not a distributed transaction. A process can still crash after the receiver commits and before the local ledger changes to succeeded. The ledger will then say in_flight, which is why recovery must reconcile or repeat with the same receiver key. A local success flag alone cannot close a remote crash window.

  A[Validate business intent] --> B[Derive stable per-effect ID]
  B --> C[Persist or load operation row]
  C --> D{Recorded state?}
  D -->|Succeeded| E[Reuse stored result; skip write]
  D -->|Prepared and claimed| F[Dispatch with same receiver key]
  D -->|In flight or unknown| G[Query receiver or reconcile]
  G -->|Committed| H[Record success and result]
  G -->|Definitely not committed| F
  G -->|Still uncertain| I[Human queue; preserve unknown]
  F --> J{Response outcome?}
  J -->|Success| H
  J -->|Ambiguous timeout| I
  J -->|Definitive rejection| K[Record known failure]

A minimal receiver-side example

The strongest simple design is for the receiver to store the idempotency key in the same transaction as the business write. A workflow caller can then repeat the same request and receive the prior result. This illustrative TypeScript-like pseudocode assumes a database unique constraint and a request hash; it is not a drop-in library. The important point is the transaction boundary, not the syntax.

async function createInvoiceReminder(input: ReminderInput) {
  const key = input.operationId; // stable for this invoice + reminder sequence
  const requestHash = sha256(canonicalJson({
    invoiceId: input.invoiceId,
    recipientId: input.recipientId,
    reminderSequence: input.sequence,
  }));

  return db.transaction(async tx => {
    const prior = await tx.idempotency.findUnique({ key });
    if (prior) {
      if (prior.requestHash !== requestHash) {
        throw new ConflictError("same operation key, different request");
      }
      return prior.response;
    }

    const reminder = await tx.reminders.create({
      invoiceId: input.invoiceId,
      recipientId: input.recipientId,
      sequence: input.sequence,
    });
    const response = { reminderId: reminder.id, status: "queued" };
    await tx.idempotency.insert({ key, requestHash, response });
    return response;
  });
}

This design works only if the receiver owns both the action and the idempotency record in the same transactional store. If it inserts the deduplication row in one database and sends an email through an unrelated service, the same gap returns: the database transaction may commit while the email delivery remains uncertain. An outbox can make the intent durable and let a dispatcher retry, but the email provider or consumer still needs deduplication or reconciliation to make the externally visible effect idempotent.

Use a transactional outbox when a database write triggers another system

Suppose an order update and a message must both happen. Writing the order and making an HTTP request inside one workflow step cannot make the two systems atomic. A process can die between them. A transactional outbox changes the local part: the order update and an outbox event are committed in one database transaction. A separate dispatcher reads pending events, sends them, and marks them delivered. That avoids losing the intent after the database commit. It does not alone guarantee that the destination receives exactly one message. If the destination commits and its response is lost, the dispatcher can send again. Put the same operation ID on the event, and require destination deduplication or a reconciliation path.

When the destination is a database you control, an inbox table with a unique event key can suppress duplicate consumption. When the destination is an API you do not control, use its documented idempotency field if available and keep the key alive for longer than your possible retry window. If neither option exists, record the boundary and choose an explicit risk policy. “We use an outbox” is not an end-to-end delivery guarantee; it is one layer of the contract.

The following cases are a proposed synthetic test matrix dated 26 October 2026. The sample size is 12 constructed scenarios, not 12 production incidents or measured outcomes. It is meant to expose behavior before a rollout. Replace the fixture names with one of your own write steps and run the test against a sandbox, including the exact platform and destination configuration you intend to deploy.

2 DNS lookup fails before the client can connect failed or known-not-dispatched None Bounded retry; confirm transport boundary in logs
3 Receiver returns a documented 429 before processing failed / retryable None for that request Respect Retry-After, same operation ID, finite retry budget

For each fixture, assert both sides of the boundary: the ledger and the destination. A test that checks only the workflow’s final status can miss a duplicated email. Record the platform name and version, workflow export or scenario blueprint hash, destination module and version, retry settings, batch size, error handler configuration, and test timestamp. For each fault, state exactly where it was injected: before connection, after request bytes were sent, after commit, or after the response arrived but before local persistence. “Simulate timeout” is not reproducible unless you identify the boundary.

For a new workflow, this can be a manual sandbox exercise. Create a receiver stub that logs operation IDs and can be configured to drop a response after recording a write. Do not use a live customer account or send real messages during the fault test.

One fix does not solve the other.

The authors report detected retry code in 23 of 200 projects, but explicitly describe that as a detection rate because their rules have false negatives. They also note their configuration sample is concentrated in a small number of repositories and the simulation uses a particular model. Treat its figures as evidence that retry behavior deserves system-level review, not as an estimate of how often your automation duplicates actions.

Failure modes that a button cannot solve

A fresh key on every retry. This turns retries into new requests from the receiver’s perspective. Generate and persist the key before the first attempt, then reuse it for the same business intent.

A key that lives only in workflow memory. A restarted process may lose the value and create another. Put it in a durable execution store or derive it deterministically from immutable business identifiers and persist the result.

The receiver silently ignores the key. A request field is not a deduplication guarantee. Verify the receiving API’s documentation, scope, parameter matching, concurrency behavior, and retention period. Stripe, for example, documents that keys can be pruned after a retention period; do not assume a key works forever.

An incorrect “retryable” classification. A timeout after a write is ambiguous; a 400 is usually not repaired by waiting; a 429 may be safe to retry after the stated delay, but only if the destination’s contract says it rejected the operation. Model these as different states.

Google SRE discusses how retries at multiple layers multiply load. Use one owner where practical, or a shared retry budget and a claim mechanism.

A green status confirms that the configured path completed, not that the business outcome was correct. n8n notes that a retry is not available for a successful execution; running a copied workflow again can repeat downstream actions. Add output assertions and business-result checks rather than using replay as a correction tool.

Prefer a stable unique constraint, upsert keyed by business identity, or insert-on-conflict behavior. Verify that the update operation does not overwrite a later legitimate change with stale workflow input.

What to measure after release

Track the number of operations entering unknown, the age of the oldest unresolved operation, retries per business operation, receiver duplicate conflicts, actions recovered through idempotency keys, manual reconciliations, and the fraction of retries that end in a known result. Keep these measures separate from total workflow failure rate. A low failure rate can coexist with duplicate business effects, while a high retry count can exist without duplicates if the receiver deduplicates correctly.

Do not choose a universal threshold without a baseline. Start by recording the counts for a bounded observation window and splitting by destination, action type, and error class. An invoice creation and a read-only enrichment call should not share the same risk tolerance. If you set a page threshold, define who receives it, what action they take, and how the alert avoids revealing customer data.

Make the action labels unambiguous: “retry with same key,” “query destination,” “mark confirmed not committed,” or “escalate.” Avoid one generic “retry” button that hides the consequence.

title: AI Agent Status Updates: Build Progress Users Can Trust Without Exposing Chain of Thought
summary:
An agent that goes quiet for ten minutes does not feel autonomous. It feels broken. A spinner and a made-up “82% complete” label are not much better: they encourage users to trust a number your system cannot justify.

The fix is not to stream the model's hidden reasoning. It is to publish a small, evidence-backed account of the work: what phase the run is in, the last verified milestone, whether it needs a person, and what will happen next. This article shows how to build that contract for long-running, tool-using AI agents.

The progress problem is really a trust problem

Users ask three practical questions while an agent runs:

  1. Is it still alive?
  2. Did it make meaningful progress?
  3. Do I need to do anything?

A token stream answers none of these reliably. It can continue while a tool is stuck, and it can stop even though a durable workflow will resume later. Likewise, an LLM-generated status such as “almost finished” is a prediction, not evidence.

Treat status as a product contract. The user-facing timeline should be derived from workflow events your system can verify: a job was accepted, a connector returned records, validation passed, an approval is waiting, or a final artifact was stored. The model may suggest a label, but it should not be the source of truth for state.

This distinction also protects privacy. A useful update is “Checked 42 invoices; 3 need review,” not a transcript of the agent's scratch work, retrieved customer text, or chain of thought.

Start with a state machine, not a progress bar

Long-running agent work has more states than running and failed. Model the states explicitly and make transitions durable.

State Meaning to the user Required evidence Useful UI action
queued Work is accepted but has not started run record created Cancel
running A worker currently owns the run lease heartbeat Stop
waiting_on_tool The run is awaiting a bounded external call tool request ID and deadline Cancel
waiting_on_user A decision or missing input is required approval or question ID Review / answer
retry_scheduled The system will retry later retry time and error class Cancel / view details
succeeded The requested result was verified and saved output receipt Open result
failed The run cannot continue automatically failure class and last checkpoint Retry / contact support
cancelled Work was intentionally stopped cancellation receipt Restart

Avoid a vague paused state. If the workflow is paused because it needs an address, show waiting_on_user. If it is paused because a vendor rate-limited it, show retry_scheduled. Specific state names let a user decide what to do without reading logs.

Here is a compact TypeScript event shape. It is deliberately about observable work, not hidden reasoning.

type RunEvent = {
  runId: string;
  sequence: number;          // monotonic per run
  at: string;
  type: "phase_started" | "milestone" | "approval_needed" |
        "retry_scheduled" | "completed" | "failed";
  phase?: "preparing" | "collecting" | "verifying" | "delivering";
  message: string;           // reviewed, user-safe copy
  evidence?: {
    kind: "artifact" | "tool_receipt" | "checkpoint" | "approval";
    id: string;
  };
  action?: { label: string; url: string };
};

Persist these events in the same transaction that changes workflow state, or attach them to an outbox. A UI event that says “report ready” before the report is stored is worse than no event at all.

Publish milestones, not a narrated thought process

Choose milestones at boundaries where the system can prove something changed. Good milestones are stable across model versions and useful if a run resumes tomorrow.

For a document-analysis agent, the timeline might be:

  • Request accepted
  • Source file scanned and indexed
  • 42 records extracted
  • Policy checks completed
  • Three exceptions need a decision
  • Final report saved

Notice what is absent: “thinking about clause 7” or “I believe this source is probably relevant.” Those claims are neither a dependable progress signal nor an appropriate audit record.

Each milestone needs an owner. The workflow engine owns checkpoint messages; the connector owns data-fetch receipts; the policy service owns validation results. If no component can produce evidence for an update, leave it out.

That rule prevents a common failure mode: a chat interface keeps emitting cheerful prose while the actual job stopped moving. Your supervisor should detect stale progress independently of the agent. For example, mark a run stalled internally when its lease heartbeat is fresh but neither a checkpoint nor a tool receipt has advanced within the expected phase window. The user-facing text can then say, “Still working longer than expected; no action needed yet,” or escalate honestly to “This task needs attention.”

Design an honest progress model

Percent complete works only when units of work are known. A migration over 10,000 rows has a denominator. An open-ended research task generally does not.

Use one of these models instead:

Work shape Best indicator Example
Fixed batch completed / total 318 of 500 files checked
Known workflow completed phase Verifying findings (3 of 4 phases)
Open-ended work elapsed time plus latest verified event Last verified update: sources indexed
Approval flow blocked state and decision impact Needs approval before sending 3 emails
Retryable external work next retry and preserved checkpoint Retrying connector at 14:05; 18 items saved

Do not convert phase count into a false percentage. Four phases do not necessarily take equal time, and the model can loop inside one phase. If you show an estimate, label it as a range derived from similar completed runs, and hide it when the sample is weak.

function statusCopy(run: Run) {
  if (run.status === "waiting_on_user")
    return "Your decision is needed before this task can continue.";

  if (run.completedUnits != null && run.totalUnits != null)
    return `${run.completedUnits} of ${run.totalUnits} items verified`;

  return `Last verified update: ${run.latestMilestone.message}`;
}

The word verified matters. It teaches users what the timeline represents and sets a standard your team can test.

Make waiting visible and actionable

The most damaging silence is not a slow model call. It is an agent waiting for a person while the product looks busy.

An approval event should include the decision, the consequence, the safe default, and an expiry rule. Keep the payload concise and reviewable:

{
  "type": "approval_needed",
  "message": "Three customer records have conflicting addresses.",
  "question": "Which address should be used for the renewal notice?",
  "options": ["CRM record", "latest support ticket", "skip these records"],
  "default": "skip these records",
  "expires_at": "2026-10-26T15:00:00Z",
  "evidence": { "kind": "approval", "id": "apr_8f2" }
}

Never bury an approval in a scrolling chat. Surface it as a run state, send a notification only when action is required, and ensure a resumed run re-reads the approved decision from durable storage. This pairs well with approval gates, but it solves a different problem: making the wait understandable to the person who initiated the work.

Transport updates without building a fragile realtime system

Start with the simplest transport that fits your product.

  • Polling is enough for minute-scale background jobs. Return status, latest_event, and etag; back off when nothing changes.
  • Server-sent events work well for one-way timelines and reconnect cleanly with Last-Event-ID.
  • WebSockets fit collaborative workspaces where users can also approve, stop, or redirect a run live.
  • Notifications should be sparse: completion, failure, and waiting_on_user are normally worth interrupting someone; routine milestones are not.

Regardless of transport, the client must tolerate duplicate and out-of-order events. Use the sequence field, make the event stream append-only, and fetch the authoritative run snapshot after reconnecting. The UI is a projection; the workflow database remains the authority.

Build the API around a durable run record

A small API surface is easier to secure and test than a channel full of ad hoc text.

GET /runs/run_123

{
  "status": "waiting_on_user",
  "phase": "verifying",
  "latest_event_sequence": 17,
  "latest_event": {
    "message": "42 records verified; 3 need a decision",
    "at": "2026-10-26T12:04:12Z"
  },
  "actions": [{ "kind": "approve", "approval_id": "apr_8f2" }]
}

Keep sensitive tool arguments, raw documents, and internal exception stacks behind a permissioned diagnostics view. The default run page should disclose only the minimum a user needs to understand progress and take the next action.

Test the status contract like an API

Status is part of the user experience, so add tests beyond the happy path:

  1. A run cannot become succeeded without an output receipt.
  2. A waiting_on_user run always exposes a decision action and cannot spend tools until it resumes.
  3. Replayed events create the same final timeline.
  4. A reconnect receives no duplicate visible milestones.
  5. A cancelled run cannot later publish a success event.
  6. A stale worker lease produces an honest recovery state, not permanent “Working…” copy.
  7. User-safe messages contain no prompt, secret, customer text, or chain of thought. 
it("does not claim success before output exists", async () => {
  await workflow.emit({ type: "completed", evidence: undefined });
  expect(await runs.get("run_123")).toMatchObject({ status: "failed" });
});

This is also where observability earns its keep. Measure time to first verified milestone, time spent waiting for users, stale-run recovery rate, and the share of runs that finish with a useful artifact. Avoid treating the number of progress messages as a health metric; a noisy timeline can conceal a poor workflow.

A practical rollout plan

Do not retrofit every agent at once. Start with one workflow where users currently refresh a page or ask support whether a job is stuck.

  1. Define the state machine and ownership of each transition.
  2. Add durable run records and one evidence-backed milestone per phase.
  3. Replace generic spinners with the latest verified update.
  4. Promote approval waits to a clear, resumable state.
  5. Add stale-run detection and a recovery message.
  6. Instrument completion quality, not just elapsed time.

The result is deliberately less theatrical than a stream of simulated thinking. It is far more useful: people can leave a long-running agent alone, return with context, and intervene exactly when their judgment is needed.

Keep the language stable across releases

Treat visible status copy as part of your API. Changing waiting_on_user from “Needs your decision” to “Paused” may seem cosmetic, yet it can break notification rules, customer runbooks, and accessibility labels. Version the event schema, localize messages at the presentation layer, and keep a small compatibility test suite for every public state. That discipline pays off when new models, tools, and workflow engines arrive: the user still receives the same clear promise about what has happened and what they can do next.

FAQ

Should an AI agent show its chain of thought as progress?

No. Show concise, evidence-backed milestones instead. They are more reliable, safer for sensitive data, and easier for users to act on.

How often should an agent send status updates?

Update on meaningful state changes, verified milestones, and action-required moments. For long silent phases, add a bounded heartbeat that says the job is still owned, not a stream of filler messages.

Is a percentage complete useful for AI agents?

Only when the work has a known denominator, such as files processed or records checked. Otherwise show the phase, elapsed time, and most recent verified milestone.

What is the best state for an agent waiting on a person?

Use a specific waiting_on_user state with the exact question, a safe default, and a resumable approval ID. Do not leave the run labeled running.

Can polling work for long-running AI workflows?

Yes. Polling is simple and reliable for background tasks that update every few seconds or minutes. Use ETags and backoff, then move to SSE or WebSockets only when the interaction requires it.

How do you detect an AI agent that is stuck?

Track worker leases, tool deadlines, and the time since the last verified milestone. A supervisor outside the model should classify stale runs and surface a recovery state.

title: How to Use ssh-agent on Linux, macOS and Windows (2026)
summary:
You gave your SSH key a passphrase, which is the right call. Now you type it forty times a day, or you quietly removed it last week because it got in the way. ssh-agent exists so you don't have to pick between those two. It holds your decrypted key in memory, signs authentication requests for ssh, git and scp, and never hands the key itself to anyone.

This guide covers how to use ssh-agent on each platform, the handful of ssh-add flags worth knowing, the two errors people actually hit, and the settings that keep a running agent from becoming a liability.

Quick Summary: What You'll Learn

  • How to start ssh-agent and add a key on Linux, macOS and Windows 11.
  • How to list, test and remove keys with ssh-add.
  • How to fix "unable to start ssh-agent service, error :1058" on Windows.
  • Why an agent full of keys causes "Too many authentication failures", and the two-line fix.
  • ssh-agent best practices: key lifetimes, confirmation, destination constraints and locking.

How do you use ssh-agent?

Three steps, the same on every platform:

  • Make sure an agent is running and that your shell knows where its socket is (the SSH_AUTH_SOCK environment variable on Linux and macOS, a Windows service on Windows).
  • Add your key with ssh-add. You type the passphrase once.
  • Connect as usual. ssh finds the agent through SSH_AUTH_SOCK and asks it to sign the login challenge. The private key never leaves the agent process.

On Linux, in a shell where no agent is running yet:

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
ssh-add -l

ssh-agent -s prints Bourne-shell commands that set SSH_AUTH_SOCK and SSH_AGENT_PID; eval runs them in your current shell. Use -c instead of -s if you live in csh or tcsh. ssh-add -l should print one line with the key's SHA256 fingerprint.

If you run ssh-add without a file name, it tries the default identities: ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa, ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk, ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk, and on current OpenSSH also ~/.ssh/id_mldsa44_ed25519.

What does ssh-agent actually protect?

It keeps the decrypted key out of files and out of the processes that use it. Your passphrase-protected key stays encrypted on disk; only the agent holds the plaintext version, in memory. Clients talk to it over a Unix socket that only your user can open.

What it does not protect against is someone who can open that socket. The ssh-agent man page is blunt about it: the socket "is accessible only to the current user, but is easily abused by root or another instance of the same user." Anyone who can reach the socket can't copy your key, but they can use it to log in wherever the key works. Keep that in mind for the best-practice section below.

How do you start ssh-agent automatically on Linux?

Most desktop sessions (GNOME, KDE and others) already start an agent or an agent-compatible keyring at login. Check before adding another one:

echo "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK"
ssh-add -l

ssh-add exits with status 2 when it can't reach an agent at all, and 1 when the agent is running but holds no keys (it prints "The agent has no identities."). That difference is useful in scripts.

On a server or a minimal desktop with no agent, running eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" in every new terminal gives you one agent per shell, each with its own keys. A cleaner pattern is one agent per login on a fixed socket path, reused by every shell:

# in ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc
export SSH_AUTH_SOCK="$HOME/.ssh/agent.sock"
ssh-add -l >/dev/null 2>&1
if [ $? -eq 2 ]; then
  rm -f "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK"
  eval "$(ssh-agent -s -a "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" -t 8h)" >/dev/null
fi

-a binds the agent to a socket path you choose, so every shell finds the same agent. The rm -f clears a stale socket left over from a crash, because ssh-agent won't bind to a path that already exists. -t 8h sets a default lifetime for every key added to this agent; more on that below.

Where does the socket live if you don't pick one? Recent OpenSSH releases create it under ~/.ssh/agent/ with a random s.* name. Older releases, which many distributions still ship, use a random directory under /tmp instead. Either way, SSH_AUTH_SOCK tells you the real path.

How do you use ssh-agent on macOS?

macOS starts an agent for your login session through launchd, so SSH_AUTH_SOCK is usually set already and you skip the eval step. Apple's build of ssh-add adds one option the upstream tool doesn't have: it can store your key's passphrase in the macOS Keychain.

ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

To have keys loaded on first use instead of by hand, add this to ~/.ssh/config:

Host *
  AddKeysToAgent yes
  UseKeychain yes
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Two things to know:

  • UseKeychain only exists in Apple's OpenSSH. If you also use Homebrew's ssh, or share this config file with Linux machines, add IgnoreUnknown UseKeychain above it so other builds don't fail with "Bad configuration option: usekeychain".
  • Before macOS Monterey (12.0), the flags were -K and -A instead of --apple-use-keychain and --apple-load-keychain. Old blog posts that tell you to run ssh-add -K are describing that older syntax.

How do you use ssh-agent on Windows 11?

Windows ships OpenSSH as a system component, and its agent runs as a Windows service called ssh-agent. Microsoft's docs note that the service is disabled by default. Enable and start it from an elevated PowerShell:

Get-Service ssh-agent | Set-Service -StartupType Automatic
Start-Service ssh-agent
Get-Service ssh-agent

The last line should show Running. Then, from a normal (non-admin) PowerShell, add your key:

ssh-add $env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519
ssh-add -l

Unlike the Unix agent, the Windows service stores added keys under your Windows account, so they are still there after a reboot. Microsoft's guide goes as far as suggesting you back up the key file and delete it locally once it's in the agent. If you do that, make sure the backup really exists first: the agent will not give the private key back to you.

How do you fix "unable to start ssh-agent service, error :1058"?

Error 1058 is Windows saying the service can't be started because it is disabled. That's the default state of ssh-agent, so this error almost always means nobody ran the Set-Service line above. Open PowerShell as administrator, run:

Get-Service ssh-agent | Set-Service -StartupType Automatic
Start-Service ssh-agent

and try ssh-add again. Use -StartupType Manual instead if you'd rather start the service yourself each time.

Why does Git on Windows keep asking for my passphrase?

Git for Windows can bring its own ssh.exe (from its MSYS2 environment). That binary doesn't talk to the Windows ssh-agent service, so the key you added in PowerShell is invisible to git push. Point Git at the system OpenSSH client:

git config --global core.sshCommand "C:/Windows/System32/OpenSSH/ssh.exe"

Or reinstall Git for Windows and pick the "Use external OpenSSH" option.
